How Taiwan's New AI Chip Export Controls Could Affect China
By CommonWealth Magazine
web only
Taiwan is preparing to impose stricter export controls on advanced semiconductors and artificial intelligence servers destined for China, a move that could significantly change how the island regulates the international trade of high-performance computing equipment.
Minister of Economic Affairs Kung Ming-hsin confirmed in an October 12 interview with Bloomberg that the government plans to add AI servers and advanced semiconductors to its list of controlled export items.
Under the proposed framework, shipping restricted AI hardware to China without authorization could become a criminal offense under Taiwan's Foreign Trade Act.
The government has not announced when the new restrictions will take effect.
The proposal represents a potentially significant development for Taiwan, which occupies a central position in the global AI hardware supply chain.
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) manufactures advanced chips used by leading technology companies, while Taiwanese manufacturers play a major role in assembling AI servers for international customers.
The new restrictions could therefore affect not only chip shipments but also the movement of complete computing systems.
What AI chip export restrictions does Taiwan already have?
Taiwan already operates a strategic high-tech export control system, including controls on sensitive technologies and restrictions involving designated entities.
Companies exporting controlled products must comply with applicable licensing requirements and restrictions on prohibited destinations or end users.
Taiwan has also expanded restrictions involving certain Chinese technology companies, including Huawei and Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corporation (SMIC).
However, these existing controls are not identical to the broader restrictions now being proposed.
The central issue is whether Taiwan can more directly regulate shipments of advanced AI hardware to China, including products that may be diverted through intermediaries.
The proposed measures would strengthen the domestic legal framework for controlling certain shipments.
They should not be interpreted as a blanket ban on every semiconductor or server exported to China.
The exact product categories, technical thresholds, licensing exemptions, and enforcement procedures will depend on the final regulations.
What is Taiwan planning to change?
According to Kung, Taiwan intends to add advanced AI servers and cutting-edge semiconductors to its controlled export list.
The measures are intended to align more closely with restrictions imposed by the United States.
Washington has limited China's access to certain advanced AI accelerators and semiconductor technologies on national security grounds.
Taiwan's proposed changes could make it harder for companies to use Taiwanese manufacturing and export channels to circumvent those restrictions.
Crucially, the government is also seeking stronger domestic enforcement powers.
Under the proposed framework, unauthorized exports of newly controlled AI hardware could be prosecuted directly under Taiwan's Foreign Trade Act.
That would differ from situations in which authorities must rely on other existing legal provisions to investigate suspected smuggling or misrepresentation.
However, criminal liability would depend on the final legal framework, the goods involved, and the specific conduct.
Why does the United States want Taiwan to tighten export controls?
The United States has sought to restrict China's access to advanced computing hardware that could support military applications, intelligence operations, and sophisticated artificial intelligence systems.
But export controls become less effective when restricted products can be purchased through intermediaries or redirected through international supply chains.
Taiwan is especially important because of its role in semiconductor manufacturing and AI server assembly.
Even when a chip is designed by an American company, its production, packaging, integration, or final system assembly may involve Taiwanese businesses.
That creates a need for coordination across jurisdictions.
In his October interview, Kung linked Taiwan's planned adjustments to commitments made under the 2026 US–Taiwan trade agreement.
Closer coordination could reduce differences between the two countries' regulatory systems, although the precise scope of the Taiwanese measures remains to be announced.
How could the restrictions affect Nvidia and Taiwan's AI server manufacturers?
The potential impact depends on the products covered and the destination of shipments.
Nvidia designs AI accelerators that are manufactured through a global supply chain involving TSMC and other partners.
Taiwanese manufacturers also assemble complete servers incorporating these processors.
A restriction covering only certain semiconductor products would have a different effect from one covering finished AI servers.
For example, a complete server may contain multiple accelerators, memory, networking components, and supporting hardware.
Regulating finished systems could reduce opportunities to circumvent chip-specific restrictions by exporting assembled equipment.
Manufacturers would need to evaluate product classifications, customer identities, ultimate end users, and licensing obligations.
However, it would be premature to estimate the financial impact on individual companies before the government publishes the controlled-item definitions.
Why has AI chip smuggling become a major issue?
Advanced AI accelerators are expensive and strategically important products.
Restrictions on their sale to China have created incentives for unauthorized resale, diversion, and complex procurement arrangements.
Authorities in several jurisdictions have investigated suspected attempts to move restricted computing equipment through intermediaries.
For Taiwan, the challenge is particularly sensitive because of the concentration of semiconductor manufacturing and AI server assembly on the island.
The issue also raises questions about the responsibilities of manufacturers, distributors, logistics providers, and overseas customers.
Existing CommonWealth reporting on the Supermicro AI hardware controversy examined how international trade restrictions can intersect with Taiwan's technology supply chains.
The proposed export-control changes would give Taiwanese authorities an additional policy instrument to address such risks.
Could Taiwan's new rules stop China from obtaining advanced AI chips?
Stricter controls could make unauthorized shipments more difficult and increase the legal risks for participants.
However, export restrictions alone cannot guarantee that prohibited hardware will never reach China.
Their effectiveness depends on enforcement, international cooperation, product traceability, and the ability to identify indirect shipments.
The final impact will also depend on whether the new regulations cover individual chips, assembled servers, or both.
For Taiwan, the challenge is to strengthen compliance without unnecessarily disrupting legitimate technology trade.
FAQs
Has Taiwan banned AI chip exports to China?
No blanket ban has been established by the announced proposal. Taiwan already has controls on certain sensitive products and entities, and the government plans to expand restrictions on advanced AI hardware.
When will Taiwan's new AI chip export controls take effect?
As of October 19, 2026, the government has not announced an implementation date.
Which AI chips will be restricted?
The government has indicated that advanced semiconductors and AI servers will be included. Detailed technical specifications and product classifications have not yet been announced.
Will exporting AI chips to China become a criminal offense?
Unauthorized exports of products covered by the proposed new controls could become subject to criminal prosecution under Taiwan's Foreign Trade Act once the measures take effect. This does not mean every chip export to China would be illegal.
Will the restrictions affect TSMC?
They could affect compliance requirements for relevant products and transactions involving Taiwan's semiconductor supply chain. The direct implications will depend on the final rules and existing contractual and regulatory arrangements.
Are Taiwan's export controls the same as those of the United States?
No. Taiwan and the United States operate separate legal systems. Taiwan is seeking closer alignment, but companies must evaluate their obligations under each applicable jurisdiction.
The Bottom Line
Taiwan's planned AI export controls are significant because they could close a gap between the island's central role in manufacturing advanced computing hardware and its ability to enforce restrictions on unauthorized shipments.
But the measures remain a proposal until the government publishes and implements the relevant regulations.
For companies operating across Taiwan, China, and the United States, the most important questions are which products will be covered, what licenses will be required, and how the new rules will be enforced.
Policy status: October 19, 2026. The proposed expansion of export controls has been publicly confirmed, but the implementation date and complete product coverage have not been announced.

articles.full_text:
Vietnam has signed a free trade agreement with Iceland, Liechtenstein, Norway and Switzerland as it seeks new markets and reduces reliance on major trading partners amid US tariff pressure.
The agreement with the European Free Trade Association (EFTA) was signed in Hanoi on Sunday in the presence of Vietnam’s top leader To Lam and representatives of the four European countries.
The deal will eliminate or reduce customs duties on a range of goods, including industrial products, fish and agricultural items.
It also covers trade in services, intellectual property rights, trade remedies and sustainable development.
Vietnam’s government said the agreement would help diversify its import and export markets, strengthen its role in global supply chains and support a rules-based trading system amid global economic uncertainty.
Negotiations began in 2012 but stalled in 2018.
The two sides resumed talks in September last year and concluded negotiations in July.
The agreement comes as US tariffs have disrupted global trade and put pressure on Vietnamese exports to the American market.
Experts say closer ties with EFTA economies could help Vietnam broaden its commercial relationships and move towards higher-value manufacturing.
Trade between EFTA and Vietnam reached 4.8 billion euros ($5.4 billion) last year, according to the association.
EFTA’s main exports to Vietnam included electrical and mechanical machinery, fish and pharmaceutical products.
Vietnam mainly exported machinery, footwear and apparel to the four European countries.
EFTA was established as an alternative to the European Economic Community, the predecessor of the European Union.
Its four members maintain close ties with the EU but are not members of the bloc.

articles.title: Vietnam just got zero tariffs in Europe. Latin American exporters should be worried. - Latin Times
articles.summary: Vietnam just got zero tariffs in Europe. Latin American exporters should be worried.  Latin Times
articles.full_text:
Vietnam did not wait for Latin America to catch up.
While South American and Mexican exporters were still absorbing the ripple effects of their own hard-won market openings, Hanoi moved — completing a sweeping trade pact with Europe's second commercial bloc one day after the rest of the world's attention was focused elsewhere. The consequences for Latin American manufacturers are not theoretical; they are structural, and they are already in motion.
A 14-Year Deal With Immediate Market Consequences
Vietnam and the European Free Trade Association formally concluded a comprehensive free trade agreement on October 18, 2026, in Hanoi, after fourteen years and 21 rounds of negotiations that began in 2012 and were interrupted for years before resuming in 2025. The ceremony brought together Lê Mạnh Hùng, Vietnam's Minister of Industry and Trade, who signed the document on Hanoi's behalf, alongside the heads of government of Norway, Switzerland, Iceland, and Liechtenstein.
President and General Secretary Tô Lâm — Vietnam's top leader, holding the country's two most powerful positions simultaneously — attended the Hanoi ceremony in person, a signal that this was not a routine trade formality but a presidential-level strategic commitment.
The scope of the agreement is broad: it addresses trade in goods and services, rules of origin, intellectual property rights, government procurement, investment, sanitary measures, and sustainable development. But it is the tariff architecture that carries the most immediate competitive weight.
Under the deal, EFTA members immediately liberalize more than 90% of tariff lines, representing 99.5% of Vietnam's current exports to the bloc. Covered products include textiles and garments, footwear, seafood, computers and electronic components, and machinery and equipment. Vietnamese agricultural goods — including rice, honey, and fruit — also receive tariff reductions. Selected European products such as cheese and chocolate will gain duty-free access to the Vietnamese market, but only after a transition period of up to 16 years.
The EFTA Prize: A $630 Billion Market With Room to Grow
The commercial opportunity at stake is considerable. EFTA's annual import turnover runs to roughly $630 billion, and Vietnamese goods currently account for just 0.65% of that figure. Bilateral trade between EFTA and Vietnam totaled €4.8 billion in 2025, with Vietnam running a €2.5 billion surplus — a gap that has widened sharply compared with a decade earlier.
For Colombian garment producers, Brazilian footwear exporters, and Mexican electronics assemblers competing for shelf space in Zurich or Oslo, the arithmetic is straightforward: their Vietnamese rivals now pay zero import duties, while Latin American goods still face standard EFTA tariff rates. The competitive floor has shifted, and there is no reversal mechanism built into the agreement.
The Mercosur Flank: Vietnam Takes the Competition South
The EFTA pact drew the headlines, but a simultaneous diplomatic push may ultimately prove more consequential for the region. Vietnam is negotiating directly with South America's largest economic bloc — not just for market access in Europe, but for preferential access to Mercosur's domestic markets themselves.
The first round of negotiations for the Vietnam–Mercosur Preferential Trade Agreement concluded on August 28, 2026, after five days of technical sessions in Buenos Aires, with Argentina coordinating the bloc's side. The framing on both ends was optimistic: Argentine officials highlighted that bilateral trade had doubled over the past decade, growing from approximately $6.6 billion in 2015 to more than $12 billion in 2025, without any preferential framework in place.
If a preferential deal is reached, the implications for Brazilian and Argentine manufacturers extend beyond export competition in third markets. Vietnamese electronics — which generated nearly $165 billion in export revenue in 2025 — would gain improved access to the Brazilian and Argentine consumer market, the very domestic revenue base that regional producers depend on when global export conditions tighten.
Latin American Textiles and Electronics Face a Structural Squeeze
For the textile sector on both continents, the combined effect of Vietnam's European trade moves represents a pincer movement.
Brazil's textile and apparel industry counts 25,700 businesses employing approximately 1.3 million workers and generating $40.9 billion in annual revenue. The sector had cautiously welcomed the EU–Mercosur agreement — signed in Asunción on January 17, 2026 — as a pathway to expanded European market access. Industry associations representing Brazilian manufacturers (ABIT), their Argentine counterparts (FITA), and Europe's own textile lobby (EURATEX) issued a joint statement in February calling the deal "essential" for competitiveness on both sides of the Atlantic.
Vietnam's EFTA deal partially neutralizes that advantage. European buyers who might have shifted sourcing toward Mercosur suppliers under the new EU framework now have an equally competitive Vietnamese alternative — one that operates under zero tariffs across both EU and EFTA channels simultaneously.
The overlap in export categories is not coincidental. Vietnam's textile and garment industry posted $46 billion in exports in 2025 and has set a $50 billion target for 2026, driven by the same European and American buyers that Latin American producers compete for. Vietnam is already the world's second-largest garment exporter. The EFTA deal adds one more preferential lane to a network that already covers most of its major trading partners.
Hanoi's Export Pivot and the U.S. Tariff Pressure
The aggressive pace of trade diversification is not a coincidence of timing. Vietnam has been under sustained pressure to reduce its dependence on the U.S. market, which absorbs roughly 30% of Vietnam's total exports. That reliance became a structural liability after Washington imposed reciprocal tariffs that left Vietnamese textile and garment exports facing a 12.5% U.S. import duty — 2.5 percentage points above the 10% rate applied to some regional competitors — according to the Vietnam Textile and Apparel Association.
Vietnam's response has been systematic: conclude the EFTA deal, push for EU-market access under the existing EU–Vietnam FTA (in force since 2020), and now open negotiations with Mercosur. Taken together, the strategy is to spread export volume across so many preferential lanes that no single market disruption — however large — can destabilize the country's export-driven growth model.
What Latin American Trade Ministries Must Reckon With Now
The Vietnam–Mercosur PTA remains at an early stage, and the EFTA deal must pass parliamentary ratification in each member country before entering full force. But direction matters as much as timeline in trade policy, and the direction here is unambiguous.
Vietnam is no longer simply an Asian competitor in Asian-facing supply chains. It is now an active rival in European markets — and a prospective entrant to South American domestic ones. For trade ministries from Bogotá to São Paulo, the question is no longer whether to respond; it is how fast a coordinated response can be assembled, and whether the advantages secured under the EU–Mercosur agreement will be enough to offset what Hanoi has just put in place.

articles.title: Helium is way more important than you might think. And the supply chain is in crisis. - CBS News
articles.summary: Helium is way more important than you might think. And the supply chain is in crisis.  CBS News60 Minutes Transcript: Helium in short supply as Iran war continues, with spot prices tripling  CBS NewsPreview: Helium Super Summit 2026  gasworldHow Impacted Is the Helium Market from the Hormuz Crisis?  Energy News BeatHelium Shortage Drives Prices Higher as Iran War Disrupts Supply  SuaraGarut.ID
articles.full_text:
The world's helium supply is facing a shortage seven months after Iranian strikes on a Qatari gas facility and the effective closure of the Strait of Hormuz. A range of industries are feeling the impact with no end to the war in sight.
While most people associate helium with party balloons and squeaky voices, this finite and irreplaceable natural resource is critical for modern life. Without helium, there are no smartphones, cars, MRI machines, rocket launches, or missiles.
Helium is also challenging to extract and transport, according to Cliff Cain, the president of a helium exploration company. It needs to be kept at 452 degrees below zero Fahrenheit in transit. Once released into the atmosphere, that's it for helium – it's gone. Cain said he's spent decades warning that the complicated supply chain is vulnerable to disruption, with the helium supply concentrated in too few locations: Algeria, Poland, Russia, Qatar and the United States, with the bulk coming from the latter two countries.
"All it takes is a few of those to fall and the whole supply chain comes unraveled," he said.
What does the Iran war have to do with helium?
The closure of the Strait of Hormuz in February trapped one-third of the global helium supply in the Persian Gulf. Then, , the facility that produces all that helium in Qatar, was hit by Iranian strikes in March, further rattling supply chains.
Ras Laffan is the world's largest facility for natural gas, and its byproduct, helium. After the strikes, the Qataris said it would take at least three years to get the facility back in full operation. Ras Laffan did not respond to requests for comment about the extent of the damage to the helium infrastructure specifically.
Qatar is the second largest producer of commercial helium in the world after the U.S. Most of the U.S. helium comes from a single Wyoming facility, according to the Wyoming Energy Authority, and U.S. helium exports are up 70% since the war began, according to export data from the US Census Bureau.
But the U.S. can't offset the shortage indefinitely, and the longer the war with Iran continues, the tighter the global supply chain of helium gets. Spot prices on helium have tripled since the start of the war, according to Rich Brooke, a former executive at Air Liquide, one of the six major international helium suppliers.
Companies in South Korea, Taiwan and Singapore are now looking to the U.S. for helium, and it's not clear how long the U.S. can accommodate that demand. It depends on how long the war lasts. For now, some helium suppliers are drawing from their reserves, which are stored in deep, underground salt caverns.
"If you can tell me what's going to happen in the Strait of Hormuz between now and three months from now, I can tell you exactly what'll be happening in the helium business. Unfortunately, you can't, and so I can't," Brooke said.
Helium: More than something for balloons
With war ongoing, the Pentagon has asked some defense contractors to quadruple their production capacities of certain weapons. That worries Cliff Cain because helium is needed for weapons development, he says.
"You can't make modern warfare without helium. And that's just a fact," Cain said. "You've heard about the missiles, the hypersonics. Without helium, you can't make the fiber optics. You can't produce the munitions. You can't produce the electronics that goes on these things. And so if you don't have helium, your opportunity to make war becomes even more difficult."
The nonrenewable natural resource is also used in scientific research, including at Joe Sachleben's University of Chicago lab. The lab uses helium in nuclear magnetic resonance machines to develop breast cancer drugs, immunotherapies and treatments for Alzheimer's disease.
While helium is naturally a gas, it becomes a liquid if it gets cold enough — the coldest on Earth. Every couple of months, Sachleben pours 100 liters (roughly 26 gallons) of helium onto magnets in the lab to stabilize them at 452 degrees below zero.
"Once it gets to a critical level, we have to put helium back in the magnet to keep it cold," he said. "If that doesn't happen, we break the magnet"
There's no substitute, no work-around.
Helium is also critical for many electronics. One-fifth of the world's helium is consumed by the semiconductor industry, according to the Compressed Gas Association. Polar Semiconductors outside Minneapolis manufactures chips for car engine systems, servers in data centers and the U.S. military.
Around 40-50% of the machines in a fab, the ultra clean area where they manufacture the semiconductors, use helium in some way, according to Polar's President and COO Surya Iyer. Hundreds of steps in the process involve helium. No helium? Everything gets shut down.
The helium crisis is hitting at a time when Polar is planning to double production capacity to roughly 140 million chips a month.
"The AI data centers are growing [a] lot of demand for semiconductors. Electrification is growing demand for semiconductors," Iyer said. "And that means the demand for helium is going to be growing for a long time."
What's being done about the limited helium supplies
Polar is able to hedge its helium reserves by relying on three suppliers. Still, the company has felt the effects of the shortage. One of its suppliers has put them on allocation — essentially a rationing program.
Sachleben's supplier also hit his lab with the rationing plan.
"They basically have said, 'Well, we'll give you 50% of what you used last year.' That doesn't help us," Sachleben said. "And so what we have to do is decide which machines are we going to sacrifice and which one are we going to try to keep."
His lab found a backup supplier, but that supplier is unable to guarantee helium deliveries. Then last month, he got a message saying that supplier was about to run out. Sachleben said he's not feeling hopeful about getting the helium he needs as the war in Iran continues.
"I don't see an end to the current conflict," he said. "And even if we do have an end to the conflict, it'll take a while for the supply lines to get going again."

articles.title: How Import Tariffs Could Impact Nebraska Grocery Bills - News-Press NOW
articles.summary: How Import Tariffs Could Impact Nebraska Grocery Bills  News-Press NOW
articles.full_text:
From morning coffee and orange juice to fresh fruit, seafood, beef, and chocolate, many staples in American kitchens depend heavily on imports. That makes food prices particularly sensitive to changes in U.S. trade policy. Tariffs are taxes collected from U.S. companies when they import goods from abroad, increasing the cost of bringing affected products into the country. While businesses and foreign suppliers can absorb some of that added expense, research from the Federal Reserve has found that the tariffs imposed in 2025 pushed up retail prices, with those increases developing gradually as higher import costs worked their way through supply chains and onto store shelves. For American households, that means tariffs on food and beverages can show up where they are especially difficult to avoid: the grocery bill.
That risk has grown as tariffs have become a central feature of U.S. trade policy under President Donald Trump. Since returning to office in January 2025, Trump has used tariffs to pursue a range of economic and foreign-policy objectives, resulting in new or higher duties on goods from many of the countries that supply American consumers. The specific policies and rates have changed considerably amid negotiations and legal challenges, including a Supreme Court ruling in February 2026 that invalidated tariffs imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA). Following the ruling, the administration temporarily replaced those duties with a 10% Section 122 surcharge, which expired in July 2026 by statutory limit and was succeeded by new Section 301 tariffs of 10% to 12.5%. But tariffs remain at an average effective rate of 6.7% as of July 2026, according to the Penn Wharton Budget Model, which is nearly triple the 2.3% average from before Trump returned to office, and that matters for the food supply. The U.S. imported over $219 billion in agricultural products in 2025, including large quantities of fruits and vegetables, coffee, cocoa, beef, alcoholic beverages, and processed foods. Many of these products are imported because they cannot be grown domestically at sufficient scale, are needed to maintain year-round supplies, or can be produced more economically abroad.

articles.title: Ban Shein and Temu: South African Unions Push for Restrictions - Condia
articles.summary: Ban Shein and Temu: South African Unions Push for Restrictions  Condia
articles.full_text:
South Africa’s largest trade union federation, the Congress of South African Trade Unions (COSATU), has backed a campaign to ban Shein and Temu over concerns that the online shopping platforms are hurting local businesses and putting jobs at risk.
The decision was taken at COSATU’s 15th National Congress, following a recommendation by the Southern African Clothing and Textile Workers’ Union (SACTWU).
The unions argue that restricting the platforms would help local clothing manufacturers and retailers compete with cheaper imported goods and create more jobs.
However, the National Clothing Retail Federation of South Africa has warned against an outright ban, saying the government should address the wider problems affecting competition in the retail industry.
Shein and Temu’s growing market
Shein entered South Africa in 2020, while Temu followed in 2024. Both platforms have attracted customers with low prices, a wide range of products, and aggressive online marketing.
Their growth has raised concerns among local businesses, particularly clothing and textile manufacturers that struggle to compete with the prices of imported goods.
A study commissioned by the Localisation Support Fund (LSF) found that Shein and Temu recorded combined sales of about R7.3 billion ($444.1 million) in South Africa in 2024.
The study estimated that the platforms accounted for 3.6% of the country’s retail clothing, textile, footwear, and leather market. They also represented 37% of online sales in the sector.
Both companies were founded in China and maintain large manufacturing operations there. Their business models allow them to sell a wide range of products directly to customers, often at prices that local retailers find difficult to match.
Thousands of jobs could be affected
The impact on local employment is a major reason behind the calls for a ban.
According to the LSF study, the growth of offshore online retailers was linked to an estimated R960 million ($58.4 million) in lost local manufacturing sales between 2020 and 2024.
The study also estimated that 2,818 manufacturing jobs and 5,282 retail jobs that might otherwise have been created were displaced during the period.
It warned that the impact could grow over the coming years. Under its worst-case scenario, more than 34,000 jobs in the retail and manufacturing parts of the clothing and textile sector could be displaced by 2030.
The figure is a projection, not a count of jobs already lost.
The findings have added to pressure on the government to protect local businesses from competition with offshore retailers.
Retail industry warns against a ban
Despite these concerns, the National Clothing Retail Federation of South Africa believes an outright ban may not be the best solution.
Speaking to CapeTalk, the federation’s executive director, Michael Lawrence, described a ban as a one-sided response to a problem with several causes.
He said the government should take a closer look at how Shein, Temu, and other offshore retailers operate in the country and whether they follow the same rules as local businesses.
Lawrence also warned that banning the platforms could reduce competition in the retail market.
However, he acknowledged that the concerns about jobs were reasonable and that the growth of offshore online retailers had affected employment in both manufacturing and retail.
Questions over taxes and import duties
In August 2024, the South African Revenue Service (SARS) announced that value-added tax (VAT) would apply to imported goods worth less than R500 ($30.42).
The change followed concerns that some importers selling goods through e-commerce platforms were not paying the required VAT and customs duties.
Before the change, certain low-value imports benefited from tax treatment that gave offshore sellers an advantage over local retailers.
Lawrence said the industry was still unsure whether the changes had solved the problem.
He told CapeTalk that some invoices he had seen raised questions about whether the correct taxes and duties were being paid. He acknowledged, however, that the invoices might not show the full amounts eventually paid.
The concerns have increased calls for better enforcement of existing rules rather than relying only on a ban.
Consumers also face a difficult choice
Shein and Temu offers South Africans an affordable way to buy clothing and other products at a time when household budgets are under pressure.
Online shopping can also save consumers the time and transport costs involved in travelling to physical stores.
Lawrence said consumers were free to decide where to spend their money. He added that households should not be expected to bear the cost of problems that businesses and government could address through better policies.
He also raised concerns about consumer protection, noting that customers may find it harder to understand or enforce their rights when buying from offshore sellers than when dealing with local retailers. Meanwhile, South Africa’s online shopping market continues to grow.
The LSF study estimated that e-commerce penetration rose from 2.4% in 2015 to 9.9% in 2024. However, this remained below the global average of 35.6% and levels recorded in countries such as Brazil and Vietnam.
The study pointed to delivery challenges and consumer habits that favour physical shops as some of the factors affecting the local market.
Government yet to announce a ban
COSATU’s decision adds weight to the campaign against Shein and Temu, but it does not mean the platforms have been banned.
The union federation is calling for a ban, while the retail industry wants the government to examine tax compliance, competition, and consumer protection more closely.
The government now faces competing demands: protecting local jobs and businesses while preserving consumer choice and access to affordable goods.
How it responds could shape the future of cross-border online shopping in South Africa.

Vietnam, EFTA Sign FTA After 14 Years of Talks, Lowering Tariff Barriers
Vietnam and the European Free Trade Association (EFTA) signed a free trade agreement (FTA) 14 years after beginning negotiations in 2012. With U.S. tariff policies increasing uncertainty in global trade, the agreement is seen as an effort by both sides to diversify their trading partners.
Vietnam's Ministry of Industry and Trade said on October 18 local time that it had signed the FTA with EFTA in the capital, Hanoi. To Lam, Vietnam's Communist Party General Secretary and State President, attended the signing ceremony. Le Manh Hung, Vietnam's Minister of Industry and Trade, and representatives of EFTA member states, including Swiss President Guy Parmelin, also attended.
Vietnamese National Assembly Chairman Tran Thanh Man delivers greetings to National Assembly Speaker Cho Jungsik during a meeting between the speakers of the South Korean and Vietnamese national assemblies at the National Assembly on the 7th. Yonhap News Agency

EFTA is an economic cooperation bloc comprising four countries that are not members of the European Union (EU): Switzerland, Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein. articles.title: Tariff-ied! This Week in International Trade (October 19, 2026) - The National Law Review
articles.summary: Tariff-ied! This Week in International Trade (October 19, 2026)  The National Law Review
articles.full_text:
Key Takeaway: In the current enforcement environment, the importance of identifying tariff underpayments early has never been greater. The Department of Justice (DOJ) is aggressively expanding its use of the False Claims Act to pursue customs violations, increasing the risk of whistleblower complaints, while Customs and Border Protection (CBP) is under explicit directives to intensify administrative enforcement, expand investigations and audits, and substantially restrict the mitigating factors that historically resulted in reduced penalties. At the same time, increased use of artificial intelligence and sophisticated data analytics are enhancing the government’s ability to identify potential discrepancies in import declarations.
These developments make a robust post-entry review process essential to identifying and correcting errors before they become government enforcement matters. Where violations are discovered before entries have liquidated, importers should correct errors using post-summary corrections. Where entries have liquidated, importers should consider initiating a prior disclosure before CBP finds out about any errors, which can lock in the possibility of completing the disclosure through the payment of unpaid duties and interest – i.e., with no penalties – provided that a complete and accurate disclosure is completed. In today’s enforcement environment, proactive compliance and the prudent use of post-summary corrections and voluntary disclosures generally are far preferable to waiting for CBP — or a whistleblower — to identify the problem.
This Week in International Trade: So, does anyone really know what candy corn is made of? Or why people, who manage to live perfectly fine lives sans candy corn eleven months of the year, somehow feel compelled to buy it when the leaves start to fall? Candy corn was pumpkin spice before there was pumpkin spice.
This week’s candy corn-free international trade developments include the following:
Tariff Refunds
| • | Consolidated Administration and Processing of Entries (CAPE) refund processing continues. Aside from a few glitches, like how to handle International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) tariffs that were paid as part of prior disclosures, CAPE Phase 1 refunds continue to work smoothly, with CBP largely able to issue refunds within sixty days of receiving the Phase 1 refund request. | 
| • | CBP deploys CAPE Phase 3 for finally liquidated entries under court order. CAPE Phase 3, covering entries more than 80 days past liquidation, launched October 6th for Section 1581(i) plaintiffs who submitted importer-of-record spreadsheets to CBP by July 31. Because many law firms did not receive filing instructions until August, numerous importers entitled to refunds remain temporarily unable to participate. CBP has advised the Court that additional instructions are forthcoming, but has provided no date. At one point, CBP suggested that refunds would occur on a “biweekly cadence,” which implies that the next group could open up on October 20th. CBP appears to be using the initial filings to test the system and clear the backlog before accepting a second group. | 
Tariff Litigation
| • | Court of International Trade (CIT) certifies IEEPA refund class action. The CIT has certified a class action for importers with finally liquidated entries who have not filed individual lawsuits, generally because the refunds at stake do not justify litigation costs. Although the class action may benefit smaller importers, we continue to recommend individual lawsuits for those with significant refunds at stake, given the likely delays from appealing class certification, the time required to obtain class-wide relief, and potentially substantial class counsel fees. Individual litigation remains the more direct, certain, and faster route to obtaining refunds. | 
Tariff Policy
| • | United States Trade Representative (USTR) continues the Section 301 tariffs on Chinese goods. In a development that surprised no one, the USTR is continuing the original Section 301 tariffs imposed on China in the first Trump administration. | 
Import Regulations & Enforcement
| • | EU General Courts expands transshipment rules. In an October 7th ruling involving Chinese electric bicycle components, the EU General Court held that parts imported separately over weeks or months may be classified as a complete, unassembled product if they collectively contain all essential components. The decision could allow national customs authorities to impose antidumping and other trade-defense duties without a separate European Commission circumvention investigation, exposing European assembly operations to greater scrutiny, retroactive duties, and penalties. In the current trade environment, it would not be surprising if the Department of Commerce or CBP adopt something similar when it comes to the coverage of antidumping and countervailing duty orders. | 
Trade Remedies
| • | International Trade Commission (ITC) considers Section 201 safeguard relief for lamb imports. At an October 16th hearing, U.S. lamb producers urged the ITC to recommend global safeguard tariffs, arguing that imports, primarily from Australia and New Zealand, have captured roughly 70% of the U.S. market and caused serious injury. Since the start of the Trump administration, there has been an increase in the number of trade remedy filings, including for antidumping, countervailing duty, and safeguard actions. | 
Export Controls & Economic Sanctions Regulations & Enforcement
| • | Russian National charged with smuggling dual-use technology to Russia. Illustrating the ongoing emphasis on economic sanctions and export controls violations, the DOJ charged a Russian national with operating a procurement network that allegedly used Hong Kong front companies to purchase U.S. microelectronics and transship them to Russia between March 2022 and April 2023. | 
Non-Trade Fun Fact of Interest Only to Me: The ticking time bomb has been a Hollywood staple since the silent-film era. Alfred Hitchcock famously explained why: A bomb exploding beneath a table provides seconds of surprise, but knowing a bomb is hidden beneath a table while unsuspecting characters talk creates minutes of suspense. In Goldfinger, James Bond stops a nuclear bomb with – naturally – just 007 seconds remaining. Galaxy Quest spoofs the cliché when a spaceship’s self-destruct countdown stops automatically with one second left because – naturally enough – its creators learned about bombs from monitoring Earth TV, and assumed that this was how countdown timers worked.
Customs has its own ticking time bombs: liquidation, which generally ends the opportunity to file post summary corrections; the 180-day protest deadline following liquidation; and the earliest potential expiration, in February 2027, of the two-year statute of limitations for filing IEEPA tariff refund lawsuits under 28 U.S.C. § 1581(i). So watch those deadlines, or you might regret it. Because Customs definitely lets its countdown timer reach zero.

articles.title: 📈 Monday data: Who won the trade war? - Exponential View | Azeem Azhar
articles.summary: 📈 Monday data: Who won the trade war?  Exponential View | Azeem Azhar
articles.full_text:
Trump’s first major tariffs were introduced in January 2018 – a (very) long eight years ago. The first China-specific ones, in July that year. The aims were multiple: to reduce the bilateral deficit (which in 2017 stood at 375 billion dollars with China, nearly half of America’s goods deficit of $792 billion), target intellectual property theft and counter Chinese policies that favored domestic companies; and improve the US leverage by reducing its dependency on China.
On paper, some of that worked. But look closer, and you see that China didn’t disappear. Supply chains got a remapping instead.
Today’s Monday Data looks at what eight years of tariffs have really achieved.
Mind the label
The immediate impact of tariffs on China was a drop in the share of US imports from China. In the mid 2010s, the share of goods imports was around 21%1. By this summer, it had plateaued at around 8%.
The Chinese engineering state found a way around it — tariff-jumping investments, i.e., relocating production to other countries. A product made in Vietnam or Mexico can reach the US as that country’s export, even if the factory, or the parts that went into making it, are Chinese.
Chinese-owned factories shipped 25% of Vietnam’s exports to the US between 2020 and 2023, up from 11% in 2018-19 – imports that don’t carry a “Made in China” label. Chinese imports have dropped, but China’s supply-chain impact remains strong.
In fact, the share of Chinese value added in US imports that arrived directly from China dropped from 84% to 75% over 7 years, while the share arriving via Vietnam more than tripled.

articles.full_text:
Roaring exports lifted China’s economic growth in the third quarter of this year, with factory output growing much faster than consumer spending.
China’s GDP grew by 4.5% year-on-year between July and September, the National Bureau of Statistics of China reported on Monday. The figures were better than economists had expected and up from the second quarter’s growth rate of 4.3%.
China’s economy has now grown by 4.6% in the first nine months of the year, putting it on track to hit the government’s 2026 target of 4.5%-5% growth without extra stimulus measures.
Industrial production rose 5.5% in September, up from 5.2% in August, while retail sales only increased 1.1%, up from 0.4%.
Duncan Wrigley, the chief China economist at Pantheon Macroeconomics, said Beijing’s policymakers were likely to conclude that their efforts to stabilise headline growth in the third quarter were successful.
“Headline industrial production rose in September partly as coalmines resumed operations after safety inspections prompted by a major accident. Manufacturing output growth remained robust at 6.0% year on year in September, buoyed up by stronger export demand for electronics, AI-related equipment and autos,” Wrigley said.
“Hi-tech manufacturing output continues to outperform traditional sectors, as China climbs the value-added ladder,” Wrigley added.
However, fixed-asset investment fell 7.2% over the first nine months, property investment tumbled by 20.6%, and infrastructure spending remained weak.
Data last week showed that China’s exports surged by more than a third in September, lifted by a rise in shipments of electronics related to AI.
“This pickup in GDP growth mainly reflects ongoing export strength on the global AI/tech boom, more than offsetting drags from the Iran conflict and ongoing weakness in domestic demand,” said analysts at ABN Amro.

articles.title: Australia–US critical minerals pact turns one: Five investor takeaways - Australian Resources & Investment
articles.summary: Australia–US critical minerals pact turns one: Five investor takeaways  Australian Resources & Investment
articles.full_text:
Federal Resources Minister Madeleine King’s National Press Club address has highlighted how Australia’s critical minerals relationship with the United States is moving from strategic agreements and funding commitments towards project development and domestic processing capacity.
At the centre of that shift is the $12 billion Australia–US critical minerals framework signed in October 2025, with the commencement of construction at Arafura Rare Earths’ Nolans project providing an early indication of its potential.
For investors, the developments point to growing opportunities for Australian critical minerals companies capable of securing strategic funding, establishing processing operations and supplying increasingly important Western industrial and defence markets.
Here are five key takeaways from King’s address.
1. Australia–US critical minerals cooperation is beginning to deliver results
King highlighted the framework signed by Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and the US President in October 2025, designed to unlock a $12 billion pipeline of critical minerals projects.
“The benefits of this agreement are real, and within a year of its execution, projects we named then are happening right now,” King said.
She pointed to the commencement of construction at Arafura Rare Earths’ Nolans project as evidence of progress within a year of the agreement.
Investor significance: The focus is shifting from diplomatic announcements towards construction, financing and project execution. Companies demonstrating progress towards production may be better positioned to attract strategic capital.
2. Nolans is becoming a test case for Western critical minerals cooperation
King devoted considerable attention to Arafura’s Nolans rare earths project, located 135km north of Alice Springs.
The integrated mine and processing operation is expected to supply up to 5 per cent of global demand for key rare earth oxides used in advanced magnets, including applications in electric vehicles and defence systems.
The Federal Government’s $1.2 billion cornerstone investment helped attract private capital and government-backed investment from the US, Canada, Germany and South Korea.
King also said the first offtake agreement under Australia’s Critical Minerals Strategic Reserve had directly contributed to the project’s final investment decision.
She emphasised that Nolans would create hundreds of skilled jobs in Central Australia while strengthening Australia’s position in global critical minerals supply chains.
Investor significance: Nolans demonstrates how government financing, international partnerships and offtake support can combine to advance strategically important projects into construction.
3. Public investment is becoming essential to diversifying supply chains
King argued that critical minerals markets remain heavily concentrated and affected by structural distortions, making government intervention necessary to establish alternative supply chains.
She defended the scale of taxpayer support, pointing to the challenges Australian projects face in markets dominated by established producers and processors.
“Now, without doubt, the scale of taxpayer support is significant, but it is a package that meets the scale of the challenge given what projects in Australia confront: opaque markets shaped by concentrated market power and structural distortions,” King said.
The government is supporting projects through loans, equity investments and offtake agreements, with the intention that taxpayers share in potential returns as markets become more competitive.
Investor significance: Government backing is becoming an important part of the financing equation for strategically significant projects, particularly those facing substantial capital requirements and uncertain market conditions.
4. China’s dominance remains the central challenge
King outlined how Western rare earth processing capabilities declined over several decades while China invested consistently in mining, separation and refining.
That investment has left China dominating much of the world’s midstream and downstream critical minerals processing capacity.
“For decades, China recognised minerals processing as a strategically important industry and built it up to such an extraordinary scale that midstream and downstream global supply chains are now wholly concentrated in that one country,” King said.
She also identified China’s increasing use of export controls and restrictions as a significant challenge for countries seeking more diversified supply chains.
Australia is effectively attempting to rebuild an industry that China has developed over three decades, requiring sustained investment, technical expertise and international cooperation.
Investor significance: Processing and refining capabilities, rather than simply the size of mineral deposits, will increasingly determine which Australian projects can contribute to diversified global supply chains.
5. Australia is positioning itself as a global processing competitor
King suggested Australia could capture approximately 10 per cent of global critical minerals supply chains over the coming years, while acknowledging that such progress would not overturn China’s dominance.
She argued that Australia was approaching a position where it could become a credible alternative supplier, particularly as international partners invest in mining and processing projects.
“But now Australia is on the verge of becoming a legitimate competitor. A great deal of effort in policy, capital, and the steel-capped miners’ boots on the ground have got us to this point, and there is no turning back,” King said.
King also confirmed that the Federal Government intends to update its critical minerals strategy in the near future.
Existing initiatives include the critical minerals production tax incentive, Critical Minerals Facility, Critical Minerals Strategic Reserve and support through Export Finance Australia.
Together, these measures are intended to strengthen domestic processing capabilities and attract further investment into strategically important projects.
Investor significance: The revised strategy could provide further direction on government priorities, eligible commodities and the types of projects most likely to attract strategic support.
For Australian investors, the emerging question is which companies can translate strategic importance and government support into commercially viable operations.
The Australia–US framework may be helping establish the foundations for new supply chains, but project economics, processing capability and access to capital will ultimately determine which companies benefit.

articles.title: When Food Giants Falter: Why Global Supply Chains Are Dangerously Dependent on Key Exporters - Devdiscourse
articles.summary: When Food Giants Falter: Why Global Supply Chains Are Dangerously Dependent on Key Exporters  Devdiscourse
articles.full_text:
Global food security faces a structural vulnerability that extends beyond crop failures, geopolitical conflicts and rising commodity prices. International agricultural trade has become so interconnected that the disruption of a strategically important exporter can trigger consequences across dozens of economies. However, the severity of those consequences depends heavily on which commodity is affected and how its trading network is organized.
A new study titled "Identifying the Achilles' Heel: Using Complex Network Analysis to Pinpoint Systemic Vulnerabilities in the Global Food Supply Network," published in the journal Systems, examines these risks across global wheat, rice, maize and soybean markets. Conducted by Xin Dai, Xiaoyu Jiang, Rui Han, Zhong Li, Yongchao Ding and Ye Liu, the research draws on trade relationships among 196 economies to identify weaknesses capable of transforming localized supply interruptions into international disruptions.
The findings expose striking differences between agricultural commodities. A simulated complete export suspension originating in Brazil affected 86.2% of economies in the soybean trading network, while equivalent scenarios originating in major wheat, rice and maize exporters affected between 22.4% and 25.5%. The results demonstrate how concentrated trading relationships can magnify disruption, although they represent modelled stress scenarios rather than predictions of actual food shortages.
A global food system where connectivity can become a liability
International food trade has traditionally enabled countries to overcome domestic production constraints by sourcing agricultural commodities from external markets. However, the same trading relationships that facilitate efficient distribution can also transmit disruptions between economies, creating vulnerabilities that national agricultural policies cannot address independently.
The study examines these risks against a backdrop of increasing geopolitical tensions, extreme weather events and trade-policy uncertainty. It cites estimates from the Global Report on Food Crises 2026 indicating that approximately 266 million people across 47 countries and territories experienced high levels of acute food insecurity in 2025, underscoring the pressures already confronting international food systems.
Previous research has examined agricultural trade concentration, supply-chain resilience and disturbances associated with events such as the COVID-19 pandemic and the Russia–Ukraine conflict. However, much of that work has concentrated on individual commodities or specific shocks, leaving important questions about comparative vulnerabilities and cross-border transmission insufficiently explored.
The researchers addressed this gap by constructing separate trade networks for wheat, rice, maize and soybeans using 2024 data from the UN Comtrade Database. Each economy was treated as a trading node, while bilateral commodity flows represented connections. The analysis assessed not only trade volumes but also the importance of individual economies in maintaining network connectivity.
Researchers then examined how networks responded when countries were removed randomly or when strategically significant trading hubs were deliberately disrupted. A separate simulation tracked cascading failures following the complete export suspension of a leading supplier, using common assumptions across all four commodities to compare their structural vulnerabilities.
Across every commodity, targeted disruption of critical trading nodes damaged network connectivity more severely than random disturbances. The findings suggest that the position of an economy within international agricultural trade can be as important to systemic stability as its production or export volume.
Soybeans face a prolonged cascade, while rice suffers an immediate shock
Soybean trade emerged as the most vulnerable network in the cascading-failure simulations. According to the study, Brazil and the United States together accounted for 84.57% of global soybean exports in 2024, demonstrating the extent to which international supply depends on a narrow group of major producers.
When Brazil was selected as the initial disruption source, the simulated shock unfolded over nine propagation rounds and affected 169 economies, representing 86.2% of the network. The first round disrupted 28 economies directly connected to Brazil, but subsequent rounds carried the disturbance through trading relationships spanning multiple continents.
The simulation recorded especially extensive disruption during its fourth to sixth rounds, when 90 additional economies entered the affected category. The prolonged transmission illustrates how interruptions involving a major exporter can spread beyond immediate customers through secondary and peripheral trading relationships.
China occupies a particularly influential position in the soybean network because of its substantial imports. The researchers distinguish this demand-side influence from export capacity, emphasizing that high network centrality does not necessarily indicate dominance in supplying international markets.
Rice presents a contrasting pattern. Its trading network is strongly regionalized, with major exporting relationships concentrated around particular geographical markets. India, Thailand and Pakistan occupy prominent positions in the network, while other economies serve as important intermediaries connecting different regions.
A simulated export suspension originating in India affected 50 economies, equivalent to 25.5% of the rice network, across just two propagation rounds. Of these, 45 economies were affected during the first round, primarily across South Asia, West Asia, North Africa and parts of sub-Saharan Africa.
Unlike soybeans, where disruption accumulated through an extended chain of trading relationships, rice experienced a sudden and concentrated initial shock. Its export connections were also the most centralized among the four commodities, reinforcing the vulnerability associated with dependence on a small number of strategically important suppliers.
These contrasting results reveal two distinct challenges for agricultural risk management. Rice-importing economies may require mechanisms capable of responding rapidly to immediate supply interruptions, while soybean trade demands attention to indirect dependencies that can transmit disruption through successive trading relationships.
Wheat and maize reveal why diversified trade connections strengthen resilience
Wheat demonstrated comparatively greater resilience because its international trading relationships are distributed among several major exporters. Russia, Canada, the United States, Ukraine, Australia and France collectively represent a broader supply structure than the concentrated arrangements observed in soybeans.
The study found that wheat maintained stronger connectivity under random disturbances, with its largest connected network retaining more than 60% of nodes even after over 30 economies were randomly removed. This suggests that dispersed trading relationships provide structural buffers against disturbances that do not specifically target major suppliers.
Nevertheless, wheat remained vulnerable when strategically important exporters were disrupted. A simulated complete export suspension originating in Canada triggered three propagation rounds affecting 44 economies, or 22.4% of the network.
The disruption initially reached economies directly dependent on Canadian wheat before spreading into additional regions through indirect trading relationships. Its progression gradually weakened toward the network's periphery, demonstrating how alternative connections can limit the extent of subsequent transmission without eliminating risk.
Maize displayed a different structural arrangement. The United States, Brazil and Argentina accounted for 66.33% of global maize exports in the study's dataset, reflecting substantial geographical concentration in the Americas.
Despite this concentration, maize maintained moderate resilience in the simulations. A disruption originating in the United States affected 48 economies, equivalent to 24.5% of the network, across four rounds. The disturbance spread initially through North American trading relationships before reaching economies in the Asia-Pacific region and other peripheral markets.
The findings also highlight the importance of intermediary economies whose trading relationships connect otherwise separated markets. Disrupting these connections can fragment international agricultural trade even when substantial production capacity remains elsewhere.
A significant distinction thus emerges between maintaining sufficient agricultural output and preserving the trade connections needed to distribute that output internationally. Countries may retain access to potential suppliers yet become exposed when critical trading routes or intermediary relationships break down.
For governments, the research supports evaluating supplier concentration alongside the diversity and stability of trading partnerships. The existence of multiple exporters offers greater protection only when countries retain effective connections through which alternative supplies can circulate.
Food-security policy must move beyond national borders and uniform solutions
The research challenges the assumption that a single resilience strategy can adequately protect international agricultural markets. Different commodities require responses suited to their particular trading structures, supplier concentration and patterns of risk transmission.
For rice, the researchers recommend stronger regional emergency cooperation, including reserve-sharing arrangements and mechanisms for rapidly deploying supplies between exporting and importing economies. articles.summary: Hanoi's Industrial Promotion Department is helping handicraft products reach a wider market.  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
Along with the efforts of businesses and rural industrial establishments, Hanoi's industrial promotion activities are supporting the export of handicrafts to international markets.
Vietnam has participated in numerous Free Trade Agreements (FTAs), including new-generation FTAs such as the Vietnam-EU Free Trade Agreement (EVFTA), the Comprehensive and Progressive Trans-Pacific Partnership Agreement (CPTPP), and the Vietnam- United Kingdom and Northern Ireland Free Trade Agreement (UKVFTA). These are important cooperation frameworks that facilitate the expansion of export markets for Vietnamese goods, including handicrafts.
A typical example is the EVFTA. Immediately upon the agreement's entry into force, the EU eliminated import tariffs on approximately 85.6% of tariff lines, equivalent to 70.3% of Vietnam's export value to the EU. After seven years, the EU committed to eliminating import tariffs on 99.2% of tariff lines, equivalent to 99.7% of Vietnam's export value. For the remaining export value, the EU allocated tariff quotas with an in-quota import tariff of 0%.
These commitments open up opportunities to take advantage of tariff preferences, increasing competitiveness and market access for Vietnamese goods. With advantages in raw materials, traditional production techniques, and diverse designs, products such as rattan and bamboo handicrafts, ceramics, lacquerware, fine art wood products, and handcrafted textiles have more opportunities to expand exports.
Speaking to a reporter from the Industry and Trade Newspaper, Ms. Lai Thi Huong, representative of Huy Quang rattan and bamboo workshop ( Hanoi ), said that most Vietnamese handicraft products are made from natural materials, making them popular with international customers. After a period of export disruption due to the Covid-19 pandemic, export orders have started to pick up again in the last two years.
Acknowledging the positive signals from the market, artisan Nguyen Van Luat, owner of Luat Nhanh woodworking facility (Hanoi), said that his facility has been exporting products to China for many years. Besides traditional handicrafts, in recent years, orders have focused more on massage products. To meet the changing demands of the export market, especially the requirements for sustainable development, the facility is focusing on technological innovation, aiming for green production and reducing environmental pollution.
In reality, opportunities from FTAs do not mean that products will easily penetrate the market. To benefit from tariff preferences, goods must meet rules of origin; and at the same time comply with requirements regarding product quality, safety, labeling, and regulations of the importing market.
Meanwhile, many handicraft establishments are limited in scale, investment resources in technology, market research capabilities, and brand development. Therefore, effectively utilizing FTAs requires businesses and production facilities to proactively innovate technology, improve designs, enhance quality, and gradually meet international standards. These are also the areas that industrial promotion policies are focusing on supporting.

Industrial promotion initiatives help bring traditional craft village products to the international market.
With approximately 1,350 craft villages and villages with traditional crafts, including 308 traditional craft villages, Hanoi has many advantages for developing handicraft exports. Places like Bat Trang, Van Phuc, Phu Vinh, and Ha Thai are associated with unique product lines, creating a foundation for exploiting opportunities from FTAs.
Over the years, Hanoi's industrial promotion activities have focused on supporting rural industrial establishments in modernizing machinery and equipment, improving designs, enhancing product quality, building brands, and expanding markets.
In 2026 alone, the city implemented support for 7 vocational training courses for 245 workers; supported 10 businesses in upgrading machinery and equipment; and organized 27 training courses with over 2,000 participants. Support for product design, packaging, and the selection of outstanding rural industrial products was also emphasized, helping production facilities improve their competitiveness. Along with production support, trade promotion activities were implemented to create more opportunities for handicraft products to access international markets.
According to Mr. Hoang Minh Lam, Director of the Hanoi Industrial Promotion Center, product introduction programs at the Tokyo Gift Show (Japan), Mega Show Hong Kong, and Vietnam Goods Week in Thailand are channels that support businesses in promoting their products, finding customers, and grasping consumer trends.
Within the domestic market, the Hanoi International Gift and Handicraft Fair 2026 (Hanoi Giftshow 2026), held from October 8-11, featured 500 booths with the participation of 230 businesses and production facilities. Of these, 180 units were from Hanoi and 50 units were from 16 provinces and cities.
Through the trade fair, businesses and production facilities have more opportunities to showcase their capabilities, connect with distributors, find partners, and explore export opportunities. This is also a way to combine support for improving production capacity with trade promotion, contributing to expanding markets for handicrafts.

During the period 2026-2030, industrial promotion activities will continue to focus on supporting the application of science and technology, innovation, digital transformation , and green production. For Hanoi, linking technological innovation with product development, brand building, and expanding trade promotion channels will create more opportunities for craft villages to enhance their export capacity.
To better capitalize on opportunities from FTAs, in addition to supporting machinery, equipment, and production improvements, it is necessary to enhance the provision of market information, guidance on rules of origin, technical standards, and importer requirements. Simultaneously, continued support for product design, quality improvement, and connecting businesses with international distribution systems is also crucial.
When industrial promotion activities are implemented in conjunction with trade promotion and integration support, Vietnamese handicraft products will have more opportunities to take advantage of preferential treatment from FTAs, expand export markets, and enhance their value in the supply chain.
Hanoi is stepping up efforts to combine industrial promotion activities with trade promotion, supporting handicraft establishments in innovating production, improving quality and competitiveness, gradually meeting the requirements of the international market, and taking advantage of opportunities from FTAs to expand exports.

articles.full_text:
Hanoi (VNA) – International media outlets have described the signing of a free trade agreement between Vietnam and the European Free Trade Association (EFTA), comprising Norway, Switzerland, Iceland and Liechtenstein, as an opportunity to expand trade and investment, and reflecting efforts by the parties to diversify economic ties and strengthen resilience amid global trade uncertainties. 
UK-based Reuters, France-based AFP and Germany-based Berliner Zeitung reported that the agreement will give Vietnam more market options, diversify its import-export relations and help mitigate risks arising from protectionist measures imposed by major trading partners. 
Australia-based SBS News, Singapore’s Channel News Asia and Nation Thailand linked the deal to the need to reduce dependence on major trading partners and respond to fluctuations in global trade. 
Meanwhile, Germany-based DW, European Interest and BriefAsia highlighted prospects for expanding exports, attracting high-quality investment and accessing advanced technologies from EFTA economies. 
Stronger ties with countries boasting substantial financial resources and advanced technologies are expected to help Vietnam upgrade its production capacity, integrate more deeply into global value chains and shift towards higher value-added activities. SBS News noted that the EFTA’s population, GDP and position in global trade could bring significant advantages to Vietnam as the two sides establish free trade relations. 
BriefAsia placed the agreement within Vietnam’s broader economic integration process, following major trade frameworks such as the EU-Vietnam Free Trade Agreement (EVFTA), the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP) and the Regional Comprehensive Economic Partnership (RCEP). From this perspective, the deal will not only open up new markets but also provide opportunities to access capital, technology and advanced equipment to improve the quality of economic growth. 
European media have also highlighted benefits for EFTA businesses seeking greater access to the Vietnamese market amid global trade uncertainty and efforts by countries to diversify their economic relations. 
Meanwhile, China's Xinhua and SBS News focused on implementation provisions and market-opening schedules, including Vietnam’s 11-year tariff-reduction period, a phase-out period of up to 16 years for tariffs on certain EFTA agricultural products, and provisions on customs procedures, technical barriers and investor treatment. 
Berliner Zeitung quoted experts as saying the agreement reflected efforts to translate economic integration into greater strategic autonomy by developing alternative trade relationships rather than relying excessively on the largest partners. European Interest, meanwhile, highlighted opportunities for EFTA companies to expand in a fast-growing Southeast Asian economy, thereby boosting trade, investment and job creation. 
According to official information on efta.int, the comprehensive agreement covers trade in goods and services, investment, intellectual property, government procurement, sustainable development, support for small- and medium-sized enterprises, and cooperation and capacity-building. It therefore provides a basis for expanding bilateral cooperation beyond tariff reductions. 
EFTA data show that Vietnam-EFTA trade reached 4.8 billion EUR (5.38 billion USD) in 2025, with Vietnam recording a trade surplus of 2.5 billion EUR. This existing trade volume provides a foundation for both sides to further tap trade and investment potential once the agreement takes effect. 
Notably, the message of strengthening a rules-based trading system featured in Vietnam’s official statements and was echoed by several media outlets. This indicates that the agreement is viewed not only in terms of economic benefits but also as part of broader efforts to maintain stable and more predictable trade cooperation mechanisms./.

articles.title: Economists expect Malaysia’s export growth to taper off in 4Q as base effects fade, trade tensions mount - The Edge Malaysia
articles.summary: Economists expect Malaysia’s export growth to taper off in 4Q as base effects fade, trade tensions mount  The Edge Malaysia
articles.full_text:
KUALA LUMPUR (Oct 19): Malaysia’s export growth is expected to taper off in the fourth quarter this year as favourable base effects fade while renewed trade tensions are expected to weigh on trade momentum, said economists.
BIMB Securities maintained its 2026 export and import growth forecasts at 23.4% and 16.5%, respectively, expecting AI-driven semiconductor demand, data centre investments, resilient liquefied natural gas (LNG) exports and US tariff exemptions to support exports.
"...Growth is likely to moderate in 4Q2026 and into 2027," it said in a note after the release of the September trade growth data on Monday.
“In addition, tighter monetary policy in developed markets and higher long-term interest rates, reflected by elevated bond yields, could soften global consumption and investment demand,” BIMB added.
Malaysia’s latest export data exceeded economists’ expectations, driven by a sharp expansion in electronics shipments and stronger orders from key markets, including the US and China.
Exports rose 54.5% year-on-year to RM215.1 billion in September, according to data released by the Investment, Trade and Industry Ministry on Monday, surpassing the 39.9% growth forecast in a Bloomberg survey and accelerating from 45.5% in August.
Imports also exceeded expectations, climbing 52.7% year-on-year to RM181.4 billion, compared with the 39% growth forecast in the Bloomberg survey.
The stronger-than-expected trade export figure came as a surprise to Pantheon Macroeconomics, which had forecast a 33.3% expansion.
“For now, we see little evidence that sequential growth will slow further, but increasingly demanding base effects should eventually temper electrical and electronics (E&E) contribution to headline export growth year-on-year,” it said in a separate note.
Meanwhile, MBSB Investment Bank raised its 2026 export growth forecast to 32%  and its import growth projection to 26%. By comparison, last year's export and import growth were at 6.6% and 6% respectively. 
It expects sustained demand for E&E and technology-related products to support exports, alongside higher imports of inputs for manufacturing and investment activities.
"We expect trade growth to moderate towards year-end, while supply disruptions, elevated input costs, weaker final demand and renewed trade tensions remain key downside risks," said MBSB in its note.
RHB Investment Bank (RHB IB) also raised its 2026 export growth forecast to 34.4%, from 21.7%, citing robust year-to-date growth of 34%.
The research house expects E&E exports, a key driver of Malaysia’s strong export performance, to remain resilient for the rest of 2026, while commodity-related shipments, particularly LNG and petroleum products, should provide further support.
“We remain watchful of the uncertainties surrounding the sustainability of the AI investment cycle, geopolitical developments and US tariff policies, which could affect global demand and trade flows.
“Malaysia’s diversified economic base, deep integration into global and regional supply chains, and ongoing efforts to diversify export markets and broaden its product mix should help sustain export performance and cushion external headwinds,” RHB IB added in its note.
