-- On October 15,2026, During the Future Industries Zone at the 2026 Hong Kong Electronics Fair (Autumn Edition) — a zone jointly organised by the Hong Kong Electronic Industries Association and the Hong Kong Trade Development Council — Sara Xiao, Chairman & CEO, GREENVLOT Group, spoke to the Hong Kong Economic Herald in an exclusive interview about how expanding AI computing power is reshaping global energy infrastructure, the path for Chinese new energy companies going global, and Hong Kong's role in global new energy and computing.
Centred on its intelligent new energy asset management platform, GREENVLOT has partnered with Cyberport to launch the Greenvlot Energy-Compute Asset Alliance (Green Energy Going Global Alliance). Built on industrial foundations with Hong Kong as its international pivot, the Alliance offers members three collaborative engines: finance, innovation and technology, and branding. Positioned as a collaboration platform for China's new energy industry moving from product exports to industrial collaborative expansion and asset deployment, it brings together Chinese industry players' capabilities for coordinated global expansion, to meet upgrading needs in global computing infrastructure.
AI Computing Expansion Reshapes the Energy Landscape as New Energy Moves from Generation Assets to Industrial Infrastructure
Rapid growth in the global AI industry is making power supply a core bottleneck for computing capacity deployment. Industry data shows that electricity consumption by data centres and digital infrastructure is rising sharply. A single AI data centre's load has risen from tens of megawatts (MW) to hundreds of MW, with some planned projects at gigawatt (GW) scale. By 2030, AI is expected to drive global data centre electricity demand up by more than 50%.
In Sara Xiao's view, competition in computing power is, in essence, becoming a competition in energy infrastructure. "What the global market truly lacks is not ordinary electricity, but stable, low-cost, low-carbon power of high quality that can be connected quickly," she said. New energy projects are shifting fundamentally in positioning — from conventional "generation assets" to "industrial infrastructure" supporting the digital economy. This brings new global expansion opportunities for China's new energy industry, which has advantages in production capacity and technology.
Breaking Traditional Industry Boundaries with a Full-Lifecycle Asset Management Platform
Unlike conventional equipment manufacturers or asset traders, GREENVLOT positions itself as an intelligent new energy asset management platform, building capabilities around the full asset lifecycle and forming an integrated closed loop of asset development, asset operations and AI solutions.
GREENVLOT operates a dual-platform model: its Shenzhen Qianhai platform leads project selection, development, construction and operations, providing the real-world asset base. Its Hong Kong platform at Cyberport focuses on R&D innovation, commercialisation and capital coordination.
According to the company, GREENVLOT has built a pipeline in Mainland China of approximately 7.6GWh of independent energy storage projects, including more than 4GWh of S-grade projects. In 2026, projects totalling 1.6GWh in Weifang and Weihai, Shandong Province, commenced construction in phases, providing solid real-world scenarios for technology and business model validation.
"We develop and build our own assets rather than simply trading them in the secondary market," Sara Xiao emphasised. "Real assets are the platform's core foundation. Although we operate as a platform, our underlying assets are real, tangible projects."
From Going It Alone to Going Global Together: An Alliance Model Tackling Industry Pain Points
Addressing the common difficulties Chinese new energy companies face going global, Sara Xiao said frankly that a single company going overseas can often only export products, while global competition has long since escalated into competition in overall organisational and collaborative capability. On this judgment, the Green Energy Going Global Alliance was initiated, integrating capabilities across the industry chain's upstream and downstream for coordinated overseas expansion.
According to the company, the Alliance brings together strengths in equipment manufacturing, technology R&D, engineering and construction, and financial services. Its members include leading equipment manufacturers such as HyperStrong, and technology companies in power conversion (PCS), energy management (EMS) and battery management (BMS).
Sara Xiao compared the Alliance to "a ship setting sail": "What the ship carries is the capability of the entire industry chain. Leveraging the boom in global computing power, and with energy storage as the foundation, we aim to bring China's supply chains and technologies to the world."
Financing is a common weak link for Chinese companies going global. Sara Xiao said that, drawing on the ecosystem advantages of Hong Kong, Singapore and other Asian financial centres, GREENVLOT can build sustainable financing structures for overseas projects — first addressing companies' immediate financing needs, then integrating resources to work with partners on overseas expansion.
Hong Kong as a Strategic Hub for R&D Innovation and Global Connectivity
For Sara Xiao, Hong Kong as the Alliance's starting point reflects a clear strategic logic. Beyond being an international financial centre, Hong Kong is a key node connecting global research, talent, capital and markets, offering irreplaceable value to new energy companies as a "super connector".
GREENVLOT has established an industry–university–research collaboration framework in Hong Kong, working with local universities and research institutes on long-term partnerships in storage dispatch optimisation, intelligent management and IoT data collection. Postdoctoral programmes and joint R&D platforms advance the commercialisation of research outcomes.
"Technologies already developed on the Mainland will undergo further R&D and refinement in Hong Kong before being commercialised in global markets," Sara Xiao explained.
Driven by the HKSAR Government's Hong Kong Innovation and Technology Development Blueprint and the Northern Metropolis development, a closed-loop industrial ecosystem is taking shape at an accelerating pace — linking R&D in Hetao, commercialisation in San Tin, manufacturing in the Greater Bay Area and global sales.
In Sara Xiao's view, Hong Kong, with a buyer network and international financial system spanning more than 140 countries and regions, can help Chinese new energy companies complete the critical leap from real-world validation to global expansion.
2027: A Key Milestone as the Collaborative Ecosystem Embraces the Global Market
On the industry outlook, Sara Xiao judged clearly: 2027 will see a concentrated release of global electricity demand and the peak shipping period for China's new energy manufacturing industry. As power supply capacity gradually keeps pace with computing capacity build-out, the computing industry is also expected to enter a phase of rapid global expansion in 2027.
"In this industry, there are no absolute competitors, only potential partners," Sara Xiao said, inviting global industry players to join the Alliance. Both established industry leaders and growth-stage technology companies can join, drawing on a shared pool of overseas projects and capital.
GREENVLOT was recognised at this exhibition as a "Star of Future Industries · Leading Enterprise" in the 2026 Future Industries Tech Top100, and its development path is also a microcosm of the upgrading of China's new energy industry: from exporting single products to exporting full industry-chain capabilities, and from single-company breakthroughs to building a collaborative ecosystem. Hong Kong is becoming a core strategic hub in the globalisation of China's new energy industry.

articles.summary: India a keystone for Hitachi Energy supply chain amid global power crunch: CEO  TradingView
articles.full_text:
New Delhi, Oct. 19 -- India has emerged as a cornerstone of Hitachi Energy's strategy to de-risk its global supply chain, as the company looks to diversify sourcing amid geopolitical conflicts and trade tensions, chief executive officer (CEO) Andreas Schierenbeck said.
Schierenbeck said rising demand from data centres and the shift from oil and gas to electricity across industries have intensified industrial power needs in recent years, creating a mismatch between supply and demand. He cautioned that while data centres can be built in 1-3 years, planning and setting up the power generation and transmission capacity to serve them can take around 10 years.
He added that meeting demand for power equipment requires long-term framework agreements, better visibility into demand and capacity reservations. Hitachi Energy manufactures high-voltage direct current (HVDC) transmission equipment, energy storage solutions and power semiconductors, among other products.
"India is one of the biggest markets for us. We are growing, we are investing. We are investing even more with time, so it's really a keystone of our strategy for global supply chains, because the other thing what we are doing is we want to de-risk our supply chains. It means we diversify, that means we're not producing only in one area and two areas. We want to have a global footprint," Schierenbeck said in an interview.
In July, the Zurich-based company began construction of a new large power transformer (LPT) factory in Karjan, Vadodara, which will require about Rs.2,000 crore investment. The new large power transformer factory will complement Hitachi Energy India's existing facilities in Gujarat that make power, dry-type distribution and traction transformers, as well as its factories producing transformer insulation and components in Mysore and Halol.
The company has 19 manufacturing units in India across eight locations. Hitachi Energy has emerged as a key supplier of transformers, high-voltage systems, and automation solutions for transmission and renewable projects. It also provides transformers for railway locomotives.
Highlighting that the company also serves the global market from its Indian facilities, Schierenbeck said: "We have a very easy strategy for India. We call it 'India for India and India for the world'. All our investments are actually directed in a way that we can fulfill the requirements of the local market, and that we can export. If it's transformer production or it's an engineering centre as in Chennai, where we just have hired 2,000 new colleagues, this is dedicated to the Indian market and to the export market."
Speaking of the growing demand for power components, including transformers, both in India and globally, Schierenbeck said that there is a significant gap between demand and supply, and would require long-term contracts and capacity reserves to narrow the gap.
"Supply and demand are not in balance at the moment, but it will eventually be in balance, even if it'll take probably a long time because the timelines of the different areas of what we are dealing with are completely different. Adding a data centre, big consumer, or building a data centre, in India, it requires two years, adding generation, with planning in most of the parts of the world takes 10 to 15 years and building up a factory in a greenfield way, it requires three to four years," he said.
He noted that demand in the US and Europe had slowed for about 15 years, but the energy transition and growing need for next-generation components have since driven a global demand surge, worsening supply constraints.
"15 years of no growth makes everybody in the industry cautious, especially shareholders. So, it can only build if you have a bankable business case. Now, actually, it's a seller's market. You have to come to framework agreements, capacity reservations. If our customers tell us what they need in the next four, five, six, seven years, and what kind, and we can standardize it, then we can lock it in, and we can plan for that."
According to a September report by McKinsey & Company, global transformer demand is expected to rise by around 40% by 2035 due to electrification, renewable energy expansion, data centres and rising investment in power grids. The global transformer market is entering a second phase of what it describes as a transformer "supercycle", with demand projected to grow at about 3.5% annually through 2035. Supply, however, is expected to remain a limiting factor for several years, it said.
Transformers are a critical part of electricity infrastructure, connecting generation assets to transmission and distribution networks and helping deliver power to end users. Nvidia is increasing its investments in Europe’s artificial intelligence sector, unveiling plans to back four German startups as the country pushes to strengthen its position in industrial AI.
The investments are part of the U.S. chipmaker’s nearly $10 billion commitment to invest in companies, universities and research institutions across Europe, as announced at the Invest in Germany Summit in Berlin on Monday.
The four startups are Agile Robots, Avelios Medical, Mirelo and Reflex Aerospace. However, Nvidia did not disclose the size of the planned investments.
Agile Robots develops AI-powered robots for manufacturing, logistics and healthcare, while Avelios Medical builds AI-powered hospital management software. Mirelo develops AI models that generate audio for videos, while Reflex Aerospace designs and builds satellites.
The announcement comes as Germany seeks to accelerate AI adoption across its industrial sector, with Chancellor Friedrich Merz saying the country aims to become a leader in integrating AI into key sectors.
Merz, who described the technology as a major opportunity for the country’s economy, named manufacturing, machinery and the automotive industry for integrating AI. He also urged Germany’s small- and medium-sized businesses to capitalize on the data they already hold.
“Please open your doors for AI to make use of your data,” Merz said. “This is a real secret and a real advantage for Germany to make use of all the data which is already available in our companies.”
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang echoed Merz’s remarks while highlighting Germany’s expertise in manufacturing, mathematics and science, saying that AI would strengthen rather than replace the country’s industrial capabilities.
“AI can only augment your capability, it will not replace your capability,” Huang said, describing the technology as a new instrument for businesses.
Nvidia is also expanding its collaboration with the German federal government and its “Industry 4.0 Platform,” bringing together representatives from government, industry, research and trade associations, to accelerate the adoption of industrial AI. On Monday, the government signed a joint declaration of intent with Nvidia to advance AI models for industrial applications.
Earlier in the day, Siemens had also announced new AI solutions developed with Nvidia at its factory in Erlangen, Germany. Siemens said the technologies could reduce engineering work involved in preparing production by up to 85%, while AI-powered production planning could cut costs by as much as 20%.
Huang had also visited France last week, where he announced investments in four French startups and met with French President Emmanuel Macron to discuss AI development. The Nvidia boss is scheduled to deliver a keynote address in Berlin on Wednesday.

Stronger links between farmers, cooperatives and businesses, and trade promotion agencies are key to expanding overseas markets, increasing export value and supporting Vietnam’s double-digit growth target.
Close cooperation between producers and businesses helps secure stable supplies and improve market access. For Seng Cu rice in Than Uyen, Dung Long Co., Ltd. provides seeds, fertilisers and technical guidance to farmers while purchasing their harvests, ensuring stable raw material supplies for brand development and market expansion.
In Lang Son province, the Huu Lung Green Agriculture Cooperative is seeking wider distribution channels for its custard apples. However, Director Le Duc Hai said the product needs better packaging, branding, traceability and documentation to meet modern retail requirements. Effective collection, storage and distribution are also essential for perishable products.
Similar cooperation in the Tay Con Linh mountains helps maintain the quality of Shan Tuyet tea through guidance on cultivation and harvesting, ensuring reliable supplies for businesses and stable outlets for farmers.
Trade promotion must therefore go beyond fairs and product advertising to connect businesses with buyers while ensuring consistent quality, supply and delivery, particularly as export markets impose stricter requirements on traceability and environmental standards.
Coffee illustrates the potential for greater export value. Vietnam exported around 1.33 million tonnes worth 6.03 billion USD in the first eight months of 2026. The sector is seeking to increase value through processing, branding and deeper integration into global supply chains. Trade promotion in markets such as Chile and Germany also helps businesses connect with buyers and understand consumer preferences.
Vu Ba Phu, Director of the Vietnam Trade Promotion Agency under the Ministry of Industry and Trade, said the 2026-2030 strategy would put businesses and markets at the centre of trade promotion, prioritising tangible results over the number of activities.
The strategy focuses on sectors with competitive advantages, promising markets, stronger international business connections and more effective use of free trade agreements. The ministry is also developing a national trade promotion ecosystem and digital platforms to help businesses access market information, find partners and facilitate transactions.
A programme to help Vietnamese businesses expand internationally during 2026-2030 will support business planning, participation in regional and global value chains, overseas expansion and cross-border e-commerce.
Market diversification is another priority, with opportunities being explored in the Middle East, India, Latin America and Africa alongside established markets such as the US, Europe, China, Japan, the Republic of Korea and Southeast Asia.
Phu stressed that achieving double-digit export growth requires substantive connections with international buyers and deeper participation in global value chains. Businesses must also improve product quality, ensure stable supplies, strengthen branding and meet market-specific standards to retain customers and increase export value.

articles.title: EV import tax plan tipped to trigger year-end booking rush - Nation Thailand
articles.summary: EV import tax plan tipped to trigger year-end booking rush  Nation Thailand
articles.full_text:
Thailand’s planned increase in excise tax on fully imported electric vehicles could trigger a surge in purchases at the year-end Motor Expo as buyers rush to secure current prices before the proposed new rate takes effect in 2027, according to the automotive industry.
The Finance Ministry is preparing to seek Cabinet approval within two weeks for an increase in excise tax on completely built-up electric vehicles with no Thai-made components, according to a ministry source.
The source said vehicles in the targeted category are currently subject to a rate of about 10%, which would rise to at least 30% under the proposal.
The measure is expected to take effect from January 1, 2027, although it has yet to receive Cabinet approval.
The government intends the higher rate to support carmakers that have invested in production plants and supply chains in Thailand while encouraging brands that still rely on imports to establish manufacturing operations in the country.
The Finance Ministry source said the higher tax would make fully imported EVs more expensive from next year.
A vehicle priced at THB1 million currently subject to a 10% rate would incur about THB100,000 in excise tax. Raising the rate to 30% or more could increase the tax burden by at least THB200,000, depending on the final structure.
The prospect of higher prices is expected to encourage customers considering imported EVs to bring forward their purchases before the end of this year.
Locally manufactured EVs meeting the relevant conditions would not be targeted by the proposed increase, the source said.
Thailand’s EV strategy began several years ago with the EV 3.0 and EV 3.5 programmes, which sought to attract manufacturers and establish the country as a regional EV production hub.
The incentives have attracted several Chinese carmakers to build plants in Thailand for domestic sales and exports to markets including Malaysia, Japan and Australia.
The government now sees the next stage as encouraging greater domestic production and local sourcing rather than relying heavily on imports.
Another key element of the planned reform is a revision of the way local content is measured.
The new approach would give greater weight to high-technology components manufactured in Thailand rather than allowing factors such as profits, labour and electricity costs to account for a large share of domestic value.
The proposed tax structure would broadly divide manufacturers into three groups.
The lowest rates would apply to manufacturers with local plants and high levels of domestic content.
An intermediate rate would apply to companies producing vehicles in Thailand but still relying heavily on imported components.
The highest rate would be imposed on completely built-up vehicles imported by companies without local manufacturing operations.
The government’s broader automotive tax strategy is also moving towards carbon dioxide emissions and domestic economic value rather than setting rates solely according to powertrain technology.
That approach would allow cleaner technologies, including battery electric vehicles, range-extended electric vehicles and hybrids, to receive lower rates depending on their emissions and contribution to the Thai economy.
Suwat Supakarndechakul, Vice Chairman of the Federation of Thai Industries and Chairman of its Automotive Industry Club, said the industry had been aware of plans for a tax increase on imported EVs.
However, he said the level of the new rate and the conditions surrounding its implementation would be critical.
Suwat argued that a tax restructuring of this nature should not include a grace period because advance notice could encourage importers to build up stocks and consumers to bring purchases forward, distorting the market.
Once buyers know imported EV prices are about to rise, he said, they are likely to accelerate purchases before the new rate takes effect.
This could create a “golden period” for imported vehicles at the end of 2026 but leave demand substantially weaker in 2027, potentially hurting manufacturers that have already invested in domestic assembly plants.
Suwat expects the year-end Motor Expo to provide a clear indication of the impact.
He predicted a sharp rise in EV bookings as consumers seek to buy imported models before the planned tax increase.
The rush could pull demand forward from next year, creating a more difficult market once the new tax structure begins.
Suwat also warned that some EV importers with weak sales could eventually withdraw from Thailand if higher taxes undermine their business models.
Such exits could create longer-term problems for owners requiring servicing, spare parts or warranty support.
He therefore urged consumers to consider the long-term stability of vehicle brands and whether manufacturers have established production operations in Thailand.
The automotive industry has also urged the government to introduce measures supporting pick-up sales.
Suwat said pick-ups play an important role in the grassroots economy and are widely used by lower-income households, farmers and small businesses.
He argued that recent government measures had stimulated EV demand more strongly, benefiting buyers with greater purchasing power, while the pick-up segment remained weak.
Some potential pick-up buyers seeking lower running costs were also switching to EVs, adding further pressure to the segment.
The industry also wants the government to move faster on other measures intended to promote the use of Thai-made parts.
Suwat said the EV policy framework contained several elements, with higher taxation of imports representing only one part of the package.
Other measures are intended to stimulate local-content use and strengthen domestic suppliers.
If the higher import tax is introduced before those measures take effect, he argued, the policy would not yet directly address the central challenge of strengthening Thailand’s automotive supply chain.
The National EV Policy Committee has already endorsed the principle that future tax rates should reflect investment, domestic production, local sourcing and employment created in Thailand.
The Finance Ministry source rejected suggestions that the proposed tax increase was designed to favour Japanese manufacturers, saying it formed part of a longer-term roadmap covering investment attraction, supply-chain development, local-content requirements and protection of the domestic production base.
The government’s stated goal is to preserve Thailand’s position as a major regional automotive manufacturing hub while encouraging manufacturers to create more economic value inside the country.

articles.title: AI boom reshapes Asia’s semiconductor supply chains - STAT Times
articles.summary: AI boom reshapes Asia’s semiconductor supply chains  STAT Times
articles.full_text:
Asia-Pacific’s expanding semiconductor industry is creating new opportunities for air cargo as AI and electric vehicle demand drives more frequent, high-value shipments across increasingly dispersed production networks.
Artificial intelligence (AI) and electric vehicles are expanding demand for Asia-Pacific semiconductors while distributing production across more specialised hubs. For air cargo, the opportunity extends from urgent chips and wafers to the servers, equipment and spare parts supporting that growth. Capturing it will depend on frequent cross-border connections, precise handling and visibility across supply chains where a delayed component can stop production.
These findings emerge from From AI to EVs: How APAC Semiconductors Drive the Global Innovation Map, prepared by Frost & Sullivan for FedEx and released in October 2026.
A broader cargo opportunity
The report identifies AI and high-performance computing as the fastest-growing demand drivers. AI accelerators (GPU/ASIC chips for AI) accounted for roughly 20% of chip sales in 2024, while approximately 2,000 data centres are expected to be added worldwide between 2026 and 2035.
The resulting logistics requirement reaches beyond semiconductor shipments. Data centres also need high-density server racks, modular liquid-cooling systems and power-generation hardware. The mix of sensitive components and larger equipment creates different transport and handling requirements within the same investment cycle.
Electric vehicles add another source of demand. “Importantly, chip content per vehicle is rising,” the report states. Power management, sensors and AI applications increase semiconductor requirements, while 5G networks, medical devices and industrial automation broaden the customer base.
For carriers and forwarders, this means a more varied cargo market, spanning small development samples, production inputs, and infrastructure deployments. Express air transport serves urgent prototypes and development boards; larger equipment movements require coordinated freight capacity and specialised handling. The report also identifies multimodal transport as part of the response to increasingly complex manufacturing workflows.
More borders, smaller shipments
Asia-Pacific accounted for about 57.6% of global semiconductor industry revenue in 2022, according to the report. Its significance lies as much in the links between production locations as in the scale of individual markets.
“Since a single semiconductor often requires design, fabrication, and packaging in different hubs, there is increased cross-border movement of prototypes, test wafers, and high-value spares,” the report says.
That pattern makes shipment frequency and connections between factories central to the air cargo opportunity. The report describes a shift towards smaller, customised consignments, requiring flexible schedules rather than dependence on large bulk orders.
Taiwan’s semiconductor exports reached nearly $170 billion in 2025, growing at a compound annual rate of about 7.7% since 2006, according to the report. Vietnam’s exports grew much faster from a smaller base, at approximately 31.8% annually.
On the import side, Singapore exceeded $105 billion in 2025 and led the economies shown in the report’s comparison. Vietnam again recorded the fastest growth, at approximately 30% annually. Together, they illustrate established trading hubs operating alongside rapidly expanding manufacturing locations.
Specialisation shapes the network
The region’s production geography explains why semiconductor logistics involves repeated cross-border movements. Taiwan and South Korea lead advanced fabrication, Japan supplies critical materials and equipment, and China combines materials supply, manufacturing capacity and a large customer market. India is a major design and engineering hub while investing in fabrication.
Before a chip reaches a customer, the chain draws on wafers, gases, chemicals, substrates and photoresists; design and verification services; fabrication equipment; and packaging and testing capacity. Finished chips then enter servers, vehicles and industrial electronics. Distribution hubs position inventory and coordinate deliveries across these stages.
Southeast Asia provides much of the assembly, packaging and testing network. Malaysia combines these activities with substrates and packaging materials. The Philippines has an established testing and packaging industry and skilled workforce. Vietnam is attracting assembly and testing investment alongside its electronics manufacturing base, while Thailand’s automotive sector supports demand for chips and sensors. Indonesia offers longer-term potential in materials and manufacturing.
The freight relationship is two-way: chips enter these locations for processing and leave for integration elsewhere. Serving that network requires connections between regional production centres as well as intercontinental export capacity.
Singapore, Hong Kong, and Tokyo also provide distribution infrastructure that links Asian production to overseas customers. As the report notes, “Modern supply chains rely on these nodes for inventory buffering and quick deployment.”
Small suppliers, critical deliveries
The cargo customer base extends well beyond the largest chipmakers. Smaller businesses supply specialised chemicals, precision parts, design services, packaging and testing, creating shipment requirements throughout the production cycle.
Design companies move prototypes, development boards and test chips between research centres and fabs. Materials suppliers need compliant cross-border transport for sensitive inputs. Equipment specialists ship repair components and refurbished parts, while packaging and testing companies require frequent wafer and chip transfers. System integrators add circuit boards and electronic assemblies to the mix.
For logistics providers, these consignments can carry commercial significance beyond their physical size. The report identifies “Time-critical shipments of spare parts and repair components to minimise fabrication downtime” as a specific requirement.
Downstream, regional distributors, freight coordinators and aftermarket providers manage inventory, repairs and reverse logistics. The opportunity therefore continues after initial manufacture, through maintenance and product support.
Resilience changes the freight brief
A more distributed production base reduces dependence on individual locations but increases the number of movements that must remain coordinated. Geopolitical tensions, export controls, tariffs and natural disasters can affect several stages at once.
The report describes manufacturers moving towards geographic diversification and inventory buffers. For logistics networks, that means supporting more trade lanes and stockholding locations while retaining the flexibility to respond when routes or production plans change.
Transport speed alone cannot resolve every disruption. “Errors in customs data or product classification can create avoidable delays, especially for time-sensitive shipments,” the report warns.
Forecast errors and upstream delays can reach factories as missing inputs. Paperwork mismatches can interrupt delivery even after international transport is complete. The consequences include line stoppages, rework and delayed finished goods.
A separate FedEx survey at SEMICON Taiwan, conducted on September 2–4, 2026 among 478 industry participants, reinforces these priorities. 35% expected their companies to expand manufacturing into additional APAC markets over the next three years. Geopolitical disruption was the leading growth challenge for 30%, while 44% identified faster international shipping as the most important capability when selecting logistics and supply chain partners.
Reliability beyond the flight
Service requirements change at each stage. Research teams need rapid prototype transfers. Foundries need secure movement of wafers, equipment, chemicals and spares. Assembly and testing plants depend on frequent international connections, while electronics manufacturers need component arrivals coordinated with production. Distribution operations require reliable deliveries and visibility into inventory across markets.
Handling must also reflect the cargo. Wafers may require shock protection and controlled conditions; finished semiconductors need secure custody. Digital coordination links those physical movements to customs documentation, production systems, and disruption monitoring.
“The ability to synchronise logistics data, shipping documentation, and real-time tracking across multiple stakeholders has become increasingly important for maintaining operational continuity,” the report states.
For air cargo, that sets a demanding brief: connect specialised factories, protect sensitive shipments and make delivery dependable enough to support production. The value of a fast flight ultimately depends on whether the component reaches the next manufacturing stage when it is needed.

|  | 
| Minister of Industry and Trade Le Manh Hung emphasized the significance of signing the Vietnam-EFTA Free Trade Agreement. | 
 On the afternoon of October 18th, in Hanoi, following the signing ceremony of the Vietnam-EFTA Free Trade Agreement, the Switzerland -Vietnam Economic Forum 2026 took place with the participation of the President of the Swiss Confederation and Minister of Economy, Education and Research, Guy Parmelin, along with numerous businesses from both countries.
 Vietnamese goods are accelerating their entry into the EFTA market.
 At the forum, Minister of Industry and Trade Le Manh Hung stated that the signing of the Agreement is an important milestone in economic and trade relations between Vietnam and EFTA countries. The bilateral FTA opens up new opportunities for cooperation in trade in goods, services, investment, and sustainable development.
 "Tariff preferences will facilitate the expansion of Vietnamese goods' markets and enhance their competitiveness; at the same time, they will help EFTA businesses more effectively exploit the potential of the Vietnamese market. Rules of origin also facilitate production linkages and supply chain connections between Europe and Southeast Asia," Minister Le Manh Hung said.
 The Vietnam-EFTA Free Trade Agreement was signed after 14 years of negotiations and 21 working sessions, demonstrating the political determination and persistent efforts of both sides. 
 On the morning of October 18th, in Hanoi, in the presence of General Secretary and President To Lam, Minister of Industry and Trade Le Manh Hung and representatives from four member countries of the European Free Trade Association (EFTA) officially signed the Vietnam-EFTA Free Trade Agreement (VEFTA).  In the context of a global economic uncertainty, the Agreement establishes a transparent, stable, and predictable framework for cooperation, helping businesses feel secure in making long-term investments.
 Minister Le Manh Hung stated that Vietnam has a dynamic market, increasingly improved production capacity, and an expanding integration network. Meanwhile, Switzerland and the EFTA countries possess strengths in technology, innovation, finance, and quality. Leveraging the complementary strengths of both sides will create opportunities to form more efficient and sustainable value chains.
 This is a comprehensive agreement covering many important areas such as trade in goods, including tariffs, technical barriers to trade, sanitary and phytosanitary measures, customs, and trade remedies.
 The agreement also covers trade in services, investment, intellectual property, government procurement, competition, small and medium-sized enterprises, dispute resolution, trade, and sustainable development.
 With its broad scope of commitments and diverse cooperation content, the agreement is expected to open up new opportunities for Vietnam in diversifying its export and import markets. This will enhance the competitiveness of Vietnamese businesses and pave the way for them to participate more deeply in global value chains. 
|  | 
| Delegates attending the Vietnam-Switzerland Business Forum in Hanoi. | 
 Meanwhile, Swiss Federal President and Minister of Economy, Education and Research Guy Parmelin noted that cooperation between the two sides has significant potential for development, particularly in advanced manufacturing; life sciences and healthcare; sustainable infrastructure and clean technology; digital transformation and innovation. These are areas where Switzerland's expertise can complement Vietnam's dynamism.
 According to Mr. Guy Parmelin, the Vietnam-EFTA Free Trade Agreement is not only a trade tool but also represents a strategic commitment to strengthening economic cooperation between the two sides. The agreement contributes to enhancing legal certainty, improving market access, and opening up new opportunities for businesses. More importantly, the agreement sends a strong message of confidence in the future of economic relations between Vietnam and Switzerland.
 Maximizing opportunities from FTAs

Preferential tariff rates, import procedures, and trade conditions are expected to help Norwegian seafood, especially salmon, enhance its competitiveness and expand its accessibility to consumers.
 Vietnam and the European Free Trade Association (EFTA), of which Norway is a member state, officially signed a Free Trade Agreement today, October 18th, marking a new step forward in economic and trade cooperation between the two sides.
 For Norway, this event is significant in expanding its seafood export market, a product group that currently accounts for a large portion of the country's merchandise exports to Vietnam.
 The signing of the agreement takes place against the backdrop of a continuing increase in demand for high-quality seafood in Vietnam, especially for products with clear origins and meeting stringent food safety standards. This is seen as a favorable condition for Norwegian seafood businesses to consolidate their position, develop their distribution systems, and gain greater access to the Vietnamese market.
 Ms. Astrid Bergmål, State Secretary of the Norwegian Ministry of Foreign Affairs , stated that over the past 55 years, Vietnam and Norway have built a strong partnership, developing alongside Vietnam's progress. Trade is increasingly playing an important role in bilateral relations, with Norwegian salmon and seafood products becoming familiar to Vietnamese consumers. 
|  | 
| Norwegian salmon is available for sale in supermarkets in Vietnam. | 
 According to Ms. Astrid Bergmål, the recently signed agreement will contribute to reducing tariffs, facilitating trade, and making business operations more predictable. As a result, Norwegian seafood, especially salmon, will have a competitive advantage in Vietnam, expanding opportunities to bring high-quality products to consumers.
 The Norwegian Seafood Council (NSC) also assessed the signing of the agreement as a positive step, creating further impetus to boost seafood exports to Vietnam. In particular, the exemption of import duties on Norwegian salmon under the agreement's commitments is expected to significantly improve competitiveness.
 Prior to the agreement, Norwegian salmon was subject to import tariffs ranging from 10% to 15%, while other competing suppliers enjoyed preferential tariffs under free trade agreements. This disparity somewhat affected the price advantage of Norwegian products in the Vietnamese market.
 Once the preferential tariff commitments are implemented, Norwegian salmon will have a more level playing field with similar products, creating room for importing and distributing businesses to expand their operations.
 In addition to tax advantages, the agreement aims to simplify customs procedures and strengthen coordination mechanisms between relevant agencies. These improvements are of practical significance for seafood products, especially fresh produce, which require strict requirements regarding transportation time, storage conditions, and supply chain stability. 
|  | 
| The Secretary of State (in a blue dress) and the Norwegian Ambassador (standing in the middle), along with the Director of the Norwegian Seafood Council for Southeast Asia (far left), survey the market at a retail chain in Hanoi . | 
 Smoother customs clearance will help Vietnamese import businesses proactively plan transportation and delivery of goods, manage inventory, and minimize costs incurred due to delays. At the same time, distributors, retailers, and restaurants can maintain a stable supply, and have more flexibility in developing menus, business plans, and promotional programs.
 For consumers, a more efficient import and distribution process not only helps ensure a consistent supply of Norwegian seafood but also helps maintain product quality during transportation. Reduced trade costs could also make it easier for more Vietnamese families to access reliable seafood products at more affordable prices.
 According to Åshild Nakken, Southeast Asia Regional Director of the Norwegian Seafood Council, the agreement opens up new opportunities for Vietnamese partners, while also facilitating expanded cooperation between the parties, bringing Norwegian seafood to more consumers.
 She believes this is an opportune time to strengthen market connections, as Vietnamese consumers are increasingly concerned about nutrition, origin, and food quality. With its existing strengths, Norwegian seafood is well-positioned to meet this consumer trend.
 In fact, despite still being subject to import taxes of 10% to 15%, Norwegian salmon continues to be popular in Vietnam. According to data from the Norwegian Seafood Council, the amount of Norwegian salmon imported into Vietnam has reached over 22,400 tons, higher than the total import from all other major suppliers combined.
 This result demonstrates the attractiveness of the Vietnamese market to Norwegian salmon, and reflects consumer confidence in the product's quality, origin, and food safety control system.
 One of the factors contributing to the competitive advantage of Norwegian seafood is the rigorous quality management process implemented throughout the entire production chain.
 The Norwegian Food Safety Authority conducts official controls from farming and production to processing, while the Norwegian Institute of Marine Research carries out independent testing programs on farmed fish before market release to check for banned substances, veterinary drug residues, and harmful environmental contaminants.
 Furthermore, careful attention is paid to processing, cooling, and transporting under temperature-controlled conditions to maintain the freshness, texture, and quality of the product from Norway to distribution points, restaurants, and households in Vietnam.
 With consumers increasingly focused on food safety, these factors continue to provide a foundation for Norwegian seafood to enhance its reputation and expand its market.

articles.summary: Vietnam–EFTA trade deal opens new opportunities after 14 years of negotiations  VOV.VN
articles.full_text:
VOV.VN - Vietnam’s free trade agreement with the European Free Trade Association (EFTA) opens up new prospects for exports and investment, with tariff commitments offering wider market access while placing greater demands on businesses to meet high standards.
      
Vietnam and the four member states of the European Free Trade Association (EFTA) - Switzerland, Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein – are to sign a free trade agreement (FTA) in Hanoi on October 18, marking a milestone in a negotiating process that began in 2012 and concluded in July 2026.
The agreement provides a framework for expanding trade and investment ties with the four developed European economies with strong purchasing power and high standards for products and business practices.
Beyond tariff reductions, the deal reflects the potential for closer economic links between Vietnam, a major manufacturing and exporting economy in Asia, and EFTA members with strengths in technology, machinery, pharmaceuticals, finance and innovation.
A 14-year journey to a comprehensive trade deal
Negotiations were launched in 2012 but stalled in 2018 after 16 rounds, before resuming in Geneva on September 8, 2025. The two sides subsequently held five more rounds of negotiations, culminating in intensive technical discussions in Reykjavík, Iceland, in June 2026.
On July 2, Vietnam and EFTA announced the conclusion of negotiations following the EFTA ministerial meeting in Iceland. The two sides had completed 21 official negotiating rounds in total. The agreement covers trade in goods and services, rules of origin, investment, intellectual property, technical barriers to trade, sanitary and phytosanitary measures, government procurement, competition, small and medium-sized enterprises, and sustainable development.
The tariff commitments are among the agreement’s most tangible benefits. Under the deal, EFTA members have committed to immediately eliminating tariffs on more than 90% of tariff lines, covering 99.5% of Vietnam’s exports to the bloc. The commitments include the immediate elimination of tariffs on industrial products and seafood.
Vietnam, in turn, has committed to eliminating tariffs on more than 86% of tariff lines, accounting for 99.9% of imports from EFTA, either immediately or according to schedules ranging from three to 15 years. The commitments are expected to expand market access for both sides, although the timing and extent of tariff benefits will vary by product.
Trade and investment: opportunities and challenges ahead
The agreement builds on an established and growing commercial relationship. Bilateral trade between Vietnam and EFTA reached EUR4.8 billion in 2025, with Vietnam recording a trade surplus of EUR2.5 billion. The figures exclude Switzerland’s gold trade, according to Vietnam’s Ministry of Industry and Trade.
Vietnam’s main exports to the bloc include electrical machinery, footwear, apparel and mechanical machinery. EFTA’s major exports to Vietnam are electrical and mechanical machinery, pharmaceuticals and seafood. This trade structure points to scope for Vietnamese exporters to expand their presence while local manufacturers gain access to equipment and other inputs from EFTA markets.
For Vietnamese businesses, improved tariff access could support exports of textiles and garments, footwear, seafood, computers, electronic products and components, machinery and equipment. The agreement also provides a basis for exploring opportunities in agricultural products, including rice, honey, fruit and vegetables, subject to the relevant tariff schedules and market-entry requirements.
The potential benefits extend beyond merchandise trade. Closer economic ties could create opportunities to attract investment and strengthen cooperation in high technology, advanced manufacturing, clean energy, innovation and the green transition. EFTA’s strengths in technology and finance could complement Vietnam’s manufacturing base and its efforts to move towards higher-value production.
However, better market access alone will not guarantee stronger exports. Businesses will need to understand the rules of origin, comply with technical and food-safety requirements, ensure traceability and meet increasingly demanding environmental and sustainability standards. They will also need reliable market information and the capacity to compete on quality, delivery and product value.
The signing marks an important step, but it is not the end of the process. The agreement must proceed through the applicable domestic procedures before entering into force, and the timing of tariff benefits will depend on its implementation provisions.
For Vietnam, the longer-term opportunity lies in using the FTA not only to diversify export markets, but also to improve product quality, deepen integration into international value chains and attract investment that supports sustainable growth. The extent to which these opportunities translate into tangible gains will depend on how effectively businesses and relevant agencies prepare for implementation.

articles.title: Temu’s business skyrockets: it goes from $290 million to over $92.5 billion in merchandise in just 3 years - Revista Merca2.0
articles.summary: Temu’s business skyrockets: it goes from $290 million to over $92.5 billion in merchandise in just 3 years  Revista Merca2.0
articles.full_text:
Temu has rapidly multiplied the volume of merchandise sold through its platform in just three years. The marketplace went from recording a gross merchandise volume (GMV) of $290 million in 2022 to approximately $92.514 billion in 2025, according to ECDB data compiled by Statista. This growth places the Chinese-founded company among the major players in global e-commerce, despite having launched its international expansion only in September 2022.
READ ALSO. Temu Is Not Just for Gen Z: Nearly Seven in 10 Visitors Are Over 34
The figure represents an increase of more than 300 times compared with 2022 and illustrates how quickly Temu has managed to scale its international marketplace model.
The metric used by Statista is Gross Merchandise Volume (GMV), which refers to the total value of merchandise sold through the platform. Therefore, the $92.514 billion should not be interpreted as Temu’s direct revenue, but rather as the value of products sold through its marketplace.
Temu Grows From $290 Million to More Than $92 Billion
The evolution of GMV shows that growth was not limited to the company’s first year of operations.
In 2022, Temu recorded approximately $290 million in GMV. By 2023, that figure had surged to $14 billion, nearly 48 times the previous year’s level.
The next major leap came in 2024, when merchandise volume reached $53.73 billion. Finally, in 2025, Temu reached approximately $92.514 billion.
Between 2024 and 2025 alone, the increase amounted to approximately $38.784 billion, equivalent to growth of around 72%.
And growth could continue. Estimates included in the report point to GMV of $125.309 billion in 2026 and $148.399 billion in 2027. As these are projections, the last two figures do not yet represent actual results.
If the 2027 estimate materializes, Temu will have multiplied its GMV by more than 500 times in five years.
Temu Is Still Far Behind Amazon in Size
Rapid growth does not mean that Temu has caught up with the world’s largest marketplaces in terms of merchandise volume.
In Statista’s 2025 global ranking, Amazon led the market with GMV of $847.35 billion. Pinduoduo followed with $780.45 billion, while Douyin reached $656.45 billion and Taobao recorded $584.84 billion.
Tmall, JD.com, Kuaishou, Walmart, and Shopee also ranked ahead of Temu. Temu recorded approximately $92.51 billion, followed by Shein with $83.48 billion.
As a result, Amazon still handled more than nine times Temu’s merchandise volume in 2025. However, the Chinese platform has already surpassed other international competitors, including Shein, eBay, and AliExpress, in that ranking.
Temu Becomes the World’s Most Downloaded Shopping App
Part of Temu’s commercial expansion coincides with its remarkable ability to attract users to its mobile application.
In 2025, Temu was the world’s most downloaded shopping app, with approximately 434.18 million downloads, according to AppMagic data included in the report.
The gap with its competitors was substantial. Shein recorded 166.19 million downloads, while Amazon Shopping reached 152.55 million. Meesho registered 131.98 million and Flipkart 100.27 million.
Temu maintained its leading position during the first quarter of 2026, with 75.7 million downloads, compared with 37.79 million for Shein and 33.61 million for Amazon Shopping.
However, another indicator in the report suggests that the pace of user acquisition is slowing. Temu’s annual downloads declined from approximately 621.36 million in 2024 to 425.30 million in 2025, according to another AppMagic data series compiled by Statista.
Mexico Becomes a Key Market for Temu’s Growth
Within its international expansion, Mexico holds a particularly important position.
In January 2026, the United States accounted for 28% of Temu’s global downloads, while Mexico ranked second with 19%, ahead of Brazil, which accounted for 15%.
The Philippines followed with 9%, Colombia with 7%, France and Germany with 6% each, the United Kingdom with 5%, Turkey with 3%, and Pakistan with 2%.
Together, Mexico, Brazil, and Colombia accounted for 41% of the global downloads included in the measurement, highlighting the growing importance of Latin America for the marketplace.

articles.title: CoreWeave’s debt is becoming the whole AI industry’s problem - The Verge
articles.summary: CoreWeave’s debt is becoming the whole AI industry’s problem  The VergeCoreWeave stock attempts to rebound on Goldman Sachs upgrade to Buy  Yahoo FinanceAI stocks bounce back after bruising selloff, CoreWeave gets Goldman upgrade  ReutersCoreWeave’s Business Is Sound Despite Debt Fears, JPMorgan Says  Bloomberg.comCoreWeave’s selloff is a lesson in ‘Finance 101’ — and Wall Street says the stock can recover  MarketWatch
articles.full_text:
CoreWeave had a bad week last week. Its bonds slipped into distressed territory by a common definition — when investors demand 1,000 basis points more in yield than they’d get from government bonds. Last Tuesady Chamath “SPAC King” Palihapitiya noticed the distressed debt, and also asked whether the AI buildout was a private credit bubble. Its shares are down more than 20 percent since Tuesday’s close, which is kind of a lot! There even seemed to be some collateral damage in the market on other AI companies, too.
Now, I have also asked if the AI industry is a bubble, but when the SPAC King echoes concerns held by a lady whose ongoing question about AI is “How are we planning on affording this, champs?”, that’s a very different signal. When I say “yikes,” it’s one thing. When Elon Musk says it, that’s something else.
When you talk about wanting to tap into the enormous sums of money that insurers have, that’s the kind of thing that makes investors afraid that CoreWeave is going to borrow even more
To make things worse for CoreWeave, Brannin McBee, one of the company’s cofounders, told the Financial Times — also last week, on the same day as Palihapitiya’s post — that the company wants to have its debt be investment-grade, rather than junk, so that it can borrow from insurers, as their capital is, in his words, “unlimited.” This is not entirely unreasonable — earlier this year, CoreWeave secured its first investment-grade chip loan. But when you talk about wanting to tap into the enormous sums of money that insurers have, that’s the kind of thing that makes investors afraid that CoreWeave — already a massive debtor — is going to borrow even more.
“The problem is not that credit profiles have changed in the last year, it’s that we’ve got another year and a half of supply coming,” Bloomberg quoted John Yovanovic, co-head of leveraged finance at MetLife Investment Management, as saying.
I have seen people suggest that this means the AI bubble is bursting. I am not so sure. A plunging stock price is not necessarily financial doom. Stocks are an expression of confidence in a company’s future, not a reflection of day-to-day business. But CoreWeave has a lot of very expensive debt, and if that debt gets more expensive, that makes it even harder for CoreWeave to turn a profit.
CoreWeave is the poster child for AI debt, and as of its second quarter earnings, owed more than $35 billion. That’s partly because it pioneered GPUs as collateral for loans, and partly because CoreWeave doesn’t have a real business beyond selling compute, a business on which it does not make money — the company lost more than a billion dollars in the first half of the year.
The anxieties investors have around CoreWeave are, in fact, present for all neoclouds
So why am I not ready to do a victory lap on this? After all, I have suggested that this business is long-term unsustainable. The answer is “remaining performance obligations” from its customers — $103.7 billion of them as of the second quarter. About 40 percent of that money is due to CoreWeave in 2028, and the companies who’ve agreed to these contracts can’t cancel them except under some very limited circumstances. Its biggest customers are Microsoft, OpenAI, and what is probably Nvidia, though CoreWeave doesn’t disclose who its third-biggest customer is. Those three generated almost three-quarters of the company’s second quarter revenue.
Microsoft and Nvidia are probably good for the money — at least, as long as it benefits them to be good for the money. (I suspect they realize that if CoreWeave goes belly-up, there will be plenty of collateral damage in the market, so they are unlikely to push the company over the edge themselves.) OpenAI is shakier, but unless OpenAI is in significantly more financial distress than we all realize, CoreWeave is probably fine for a while. As long as it can continue to pay off its debt, the music keeps going. Only when the AI boom falters are we going to find out if it’s actually a viable business.
Still, the angst around CoreWeave has made things shaky for other companies that have taken out significant debt in the AI buildout — Oracle’s shares, for instance, which have fallen almost 10 percent in the same timeframe. There’s been a sell-off in Oracle bonds, too. The anxieties investors have around CoreWeave are, in fact, present for all neoclouds. It’s just not clear the bare-metal business is a good one.

The global optical liquid level sensor market is entering a phase of structural expansion, shaped by the broader digitization of industrial processes and the increasing need for reliable, non-contact liquid detection across critical applications. Unlike conventional float or conductive sensors, optical sensors offer advantages in media compatibility, miniaturization, and immunity to electromagnetic interference, making them indispensable in medical devices, chemical processing, food and beverage, automotive, and consumer appliances.
As industries move toward predictive maintenance and Industry 4.0 frameworks, demand is shifting from basic switching functionality to integrated intelligence, including IO-Link connectivity, self-diagnostics, and contamination detection. Key findings indicate that the market is application-driven, with success contingent on deep media compatibility knowledge and navigating lengthy OEM qualification cycles.
The value chain is hybrid, requiring mastery of component innovation, modular assembly, and direct design-in support. Demand is bifurcated between high-reliability, high-margin applications and high-volume, cost-sensitive segments. Regulatory compliance acts as a moat in regulated sectors, while supply chain resilience necessitates a multi-hub strategy. The report is designed for component manufacturers, system suppliers, OEMs, distributors, and investors seeking a clear view of end-use demand, design-in dynamics, and competitive positioning.
The baseline scenario for the optical liquid level sensor market anticipates steady growth through 2035, with a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 5.8% from 2026 to 2035. This outlook is supported by the accelerating adoption of automation and smart sensing technologies across industrial, medical, and consumer applications. The market is expected to reach a higher level of maturity in developed regions, while emerging economies in Asia-Pacific and Latin America present significant untapped potential. Demand is increasingly driven by the need for reliable, maintenance-free liquid level detection in harsh environments, where optical sensors outperform traditional alternatives.
The integration of digital communication protocols such as IO-Link is transforming the competitive landscape, enabling predictive maintenance and reducing downtime. However, the market faces restraints from the high cost of customized solutions and the complexity of qualification cycles, particularly in regulated industries. The supply chain is evolving toward multi-hub manufacturing to mitigate risks, with Asia-Pacific remaining the dominant production hub. The medical devices sector represents a significant and growing application area for optical liquid level sensors, driven by the need for accurate, reliable, and contamination-free liquid detection in critical care equipment. Optical sensors are preferred for their non-contact operation, which minimizes the risk of cross-contamination and ensures compatibility with sterile environments. Key applications include infusion pumps, dialysis machines, blood analyzers, and reagent level monitoring in in-vitro diagnostics. The demand is supported by the aging population, increasing prevalence of chronic diseases, and the shift toward point-of-care testing.

They are used in filling machines, mixing tanks, and beverage dispensers for accurate level control and to prevent overflow. The demand is driven by the growing emphasis on food safety (e.g., FDA, 3-A Sanitary Standards) and the need for automation to improve efficiency. Through 2035, the trend toward smart factories and traceability will drive the adoption of sensors with digital interfaces and self-diagnostics.

articles.title: What is behind the breakdown in Western society - ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation
articles.summary: What is behind the breakdown in Western society  ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation

source_detail.name: ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting Corporation

articles.full_text:
Disillusion is rapidly turning to discontent and open conflict.
Over the weekend, demonstrators took to the streets across France, Spain, Portugal, Italy and Belgium, battling police, torching public buildings and looting shops.
The scenes have mirrored events on the other side of the Atlantic, where the political chasm dividing America has grown, with outbursts of public anger against authorities gaining momentum.
Across the developed world, including here in Australia, political momentum has shifted from the centre to the fringes in an increasingly bipolar world that, if it continues, ultimately will render any attempt at consensus futile.
Populist leaders, experts at whipping up fury for personal gain, are in the ascendancy despite offering little in the way of solutions.
While the catalysts in each country may differ, the root cause largely is the same: the economy.
The compact — the unwritten agreement — between workers and the democratic state is fraying.
Lower- and middle-income workers feel they're going backwards. And they're not imagining it.
Wages have not kept pace with inflation as asset prices have soared. Property ownership in many Western nations is almost out of reach of ordinary workers, while rents have skyrocketed.
That has concentrated wealth in an increasingly smaller cohort of wealthy households.
The cost-of-living crisis has become a transnational phenomenon.
And as prices continue to surge, central banks have responded in unison by raising interest rates, piling further pressure on those already most affected.
The cost of inequality is beginning to manifest itself.
Why you feel poor
Here's a snapshot of why workers are angry.
If you take inflation into account, Australian incomes are back to where they were in 2011.
There was the post-pandemic inflation hangover piled on top of Russia's invasion of Ukraine, which sent energy prices into orbit, that's now been followed by America's war in Iran.
The combination has not just obliterated income growth. It has sent it into reverse.
It's a story writ large across the Western world.
Just how intractable the problem has become is on full display right here at home.
The opposition and a large posse of economic commentators point to federal government spending. It's firing up inflation, they argue, and driving interest rates higher.
That's not entirely true. For a start, there are huge global forces at work. But let's look at the domestic situation.
Spending alone isn't the problem. It is the imbalance between tax revenue and spending. There's not enough tax to pay for all that spending, and the shortfall, the deficit, must be funded by debt.
There are two levers you can pull here. One is raising taxes, which no-one will ever support. And the other is cutting spending, which no-one will ever support.
From 2013 to the pandemic, Australia, a resource-exporting nation, ran up deficits during the greatest resources boom in history.
The government of the day decided to throw away a resources tax, a decision that has cost the country dearly.
And to this day, we continue to sell our resources, charging a fraction of the taxes other nations apply.
In the meantime, lobbyists continually agitate for cuts to income and company taxes, even as we stare into the abyss of ongoing deficits.
Their universal fix is to raise the Goods and Services Tax, which, if you hadn't already guessed, hits low- and middle-income earners the hardest.
Remember the three-stage income tax cuts, the ones that really benefited higher-income earners?
Apparently, they were going to be self-funding. They were going to generate so much economic activity that the cuts would increase government revenue.
Instead, they've created a structural imbalance in our federal finances.
And whenever the idea of spending cuts is raised, there is an almighty burst of outrage.
Just ask Joe Hockey. His 2014 federal budget was howled down.
This year's budget, meanwhile, targeted welfare payments to the wealthy, which, given our circumstances, should have been a no-brainer.
The hugely generous discounts to capital gains tax and the loophole created by negative gearing were wound back, along with a tightening of the generous tax arrangements surrounding family trusts.
Five months later, and the outcry against the changes continues.
Tax concessions may not seem like spending, but, in essence, they are. That's because they cost the budget as revenue is foregone while the benefits accrue to a targeted cohort.
Other taxpayers, paying the full rate, end up subsidising the beneficiaries.
And it is wealthier households that overwhelmingly benefit from those concessions.
Loading
The Trump legacy: higher interest rates
Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) governor Michele Bullock has confirmed what many of us have feared.
Higher interest rates are here to stay.
"I don't know if this particular level is the new normal, but what I do know is that we're not going back down to interest rates of zero or very close to zero, policy rates of that," she said after the RBA rate hike this month.
Inflation is no longer an Australian-only concern. It's rising across the developed world.
The US Federal Reserve has already raised rates once this year and, after hotter-than-expected inflation stats this month, could go again before Christmas.
In the past few weeks, bond markets have pushed interest rates on longer-term US government debt dramatically higher as concerns about US government debt continue to rattle investors.
Tax cuts for the wealthy, under Donald Trump's Big Beautiful Bill, coupled with huge outlays for the war in Iran, have sent US debt into orbit.
As you can see below, America's debt-to-GDP is now at 126 per cent, far higher than during World War II.
The interest bill on that debt is now the second-biggest expense in the US Budget and outstrips defence spending. With soaring US bond rates, that bill is now becoming ever more expensive.
As a much smaller nation that imports capital for investment, longer-term Australian government debt rates have soared alongside the greenback.
Add in the trillions of dollars earmarked for artificial intelligence investment over the next few years, and the global demand for debt funding is likely to keep interest rates elevated for years.
Higher inflation and higher interest bills eat into worker salaries.
When did the rot set in?
Some point to the global financial crisis (GFC).
Governments and central banks bailed out the culprits while workers were left to fend for themselves.
What followed was mass unemployment and an acceleration of the globalisation trends that sent much of the world's manufacturing industries to China.
Inflation all but disappeared and interest rates, in what now appears to be an aberration, plummeted.
Stock markets boomed and real estate soared, giving a false impression of rapidly rising national wealth across the Western world. The gap between the have-mores and the have-nots grew ever wider but was largely ignored.
But the GFC was merely a flashpoint when the tectonic forces that had been building for years finally snapped.
For decades, the great economic experiment of the 80s appeared a resounding success.
Reagan and Thatcher pushed through financial deregulation and allowed market forces to dominate, liberated debt markets, allowed trade to flow freely, increased wealth and raised living standards across the globe.
There was a dogmatic application of the theory of free markets and globalisation as detractors were denigrated and discarded.
For more than 30 years, it seemed to work, until it all blew up.
But even then, it appears we only paid attention to one side of the Yin and Yang of an economic revolution.
And now the costs are mounting.

FARGO, N.D., October 19, 2026 — Border States has published the following supply chain update.
Lead Time Trends
Canadian import ban takes effect as U.S.-China tariff reductions are announced
Several U.S. tariff-related developments occurred since September.
- Canada: The United States’ import ban on certain Canadian goods took effect in late September, while broader U.S. and Canada’s tariffs remain in place. Customers purchasing Canadian-origin products or products that rely on Canadian inputs should verify whether specific items are affected rather than assuming an entire product category is included.
- China: Following the U.S.-China summit, the two countries agreed to reciprocal tariff reductions covering approximately $30 billion in non-sensitive goods each. The reductions will take effect after both countries complete their required domestic procedures. The countries also extended their trade truce until Sunday, January 10.
- Section 232 metals: No material change to the current steel, aluminum and copper tariff structure. The Department of Commerce proposal to add 14-metal containing product categories, including certain electric conductor cables, remains under review.
- Section 301: The 10% and 12.5% tariffs implemented in July on 60 trading partners covering 99.4% of U.S. imports, remain in effect. In late September, the U.S. Court of International Trade heard arguments challenging the legal basis for these tariffs; it has not yet issued a ruling.
The bottom line: Product origin, classification, material content, quote validity and supplier documentation remain the main factors affecting total delivered cost. We continue to work with suppliers to understand potential cost and availability impacts.
Labor conditions remain stable but uneven as the Federal Reserve raises rates
Payroll growth slowed considerably from August, with 29,000 jobs added, down from a revised 133,000 jobs in August and, below expectations.
By the numbers: Unemployment edged up to 4.2%, from 4.1% in August. Wage growth softened further at 0.1% month over month. At the same time, labor force participation rose to 61.8%, from 61.6%, suggesting more workers are entering or re-entering the workforce.
Why it matters: Employment across most major industries changed little during September. While hiring momentum has slowed, labor demand remains relatively stable in many infrastructure- and project-related industries.
The Federal Reserve raised rates for the first time in three years, increasing the federal funds target range by 25 basis points to 3.75%–4% in September. Another rate hike is anticipated by year-end. Borrowing, project financing and inventory-carrying costs may remain elevated.
The bottom line: Expect labor conditions to remain stable but uneven through year-end. Labor challenges are likely to remain concentrated among electricians, utility crews, field service technicians, transportation-related positions and other skilled project-specific roles.
Transpacific rates climbed as capacity reduced
Transpacific rates hit new highs in mid-September as carriers kept capacity tight.
By the numbers:
- Drewry’s World Container Index ended September at $4,434/FEU (40-foot equivalent units), down 9% from August but still approximately 166% higher year over year.
- On the U.S. East Coast (USEC) trade lane, Shanghai-to-New York rates climbed 11.4% to $10,394/FEU by mid-September.
- On the U.S. West Coast trade lane, Shanghai-to-Los Angeles rates rose 13.1% to $7,712/FEU by mid-September.
- Carriers planned 47 blank sailings across major east-west trade routes from late August through early October, approximately 6% of scheduled capacity.
Why it matters: The transpacific has become a carrier-managed market rather than a demand-driven one. Importers did not stage a conventional peak, yet carriers held USEC rates above $10,000/FEU by reducing capacity ahead of China’s Golden Week national holiday and layering Panama Canal surcharges onto already elevated base rates.
Key takeaway: With Golden Week pausing Chinese factory output in early October and vessel delays clustering arrivals into November, U.S. imports will likely see firm pricing and schedule variability through the end of the year.
Surface market pricing pressure returns as diesel reaches record highs
September brought the brief August cooldown to an end, as surface rates turned back up and diesel prices reached record highs. The International Energy Agency expects diesel supply to remain tight into 2027 as falling inventories and supply disruptions continue to strain the market.
By the numbers:
- Spot rates: Dry van climbed 4.2% month over month to $3.01 per mile and flatbed rose 2.3% month over month to $3.62 per mile.
- Contract rates: Van rose 4.2% month over month to $3.24 per mile, flatbed rose 3.6% month over month to $4.07 per mile.
- Load-to-truck ratios tightened with van ratio rising 9.3% to 11.3 and flatbed ratio rising 8.4% to 39.0, while total for-hire tractors continued to decline.
- Intermodal: Cumulative volume remained strong, reaching 48 million units, through the first 37 weeks of 2026, up 4.1% year over year.
What this means: The surface market’s brief summer exhale is over, and the structural squeeze is back in force. Spot and contract rates rose altogether, load-to-truck ratios tightened, and diesel prices set new records, all while new capacity failed to materialize despite a year of elevated rejections.
Elevated commodity prices continue to shape material costs
Through October, copper, aluminum and steel remain the key commodities to watch, while resin and PVC markets continue to reflect strong infrastructure and data center demand.
Across the categories:
- Copper remains 31% above prior year levels despite declining 1% month over month.
- Aluminum is still 26% higher than last year after falling 3%.
- Hot-rolled steel increased another 1% and remains 57% above year-ago levels.
- PVC price increases have now held for two consecutive months, and larger-diameter conduit and pipe products continue to see extended lead times.
- Resins remain elevated, while demand from power infrastructure, electrification and data center projects continues to support overall commodity markets.
What we’re watching: Trade policy, geopolitical risks, new production capacity and supplier activity could continue to influence costs in the near term. Potential changes to Section 232 tariffs and proposed copper derivative tariffs also remain longer-term watch items.
Looking ahead: Expect continued volatility across metal-intensive and project-driven categories over the next 60–90 days. Focus on early planning, quote validity, alternative supply options and project visibility.
Bonus: Read our 2026 State of Commodities report for a high level overview of the top factors impacting commodities and what to watch for in 2027.
