articles.title: Q&A: How U.S. Trade Policies Are Reshaping Chinese Robotics Imports - Automation World
articles.summary: Q&A: How U.S. Trade Policies Are Reshaping Chinese Robotics Imports  Automation World
articles.full_text:
From an investor perspective, that changes the way we think about things. Companies can no longer look at a robot simply on the basis of purchase price, performance and availability. They increasingly have to think about tariffs, supply chain exposure, component sourcing, cybersecurity, geopolitical risk and the possibility that today's acceptable supplier could face new restrictions tomorrow.
On the FCC action, I think it was a necessary move, but it isn't a strategy on its own. China has been explicit about its robotics roadmap for years. We haven't. A pause like this only pays off if we use it to build a national robotics strategy with real input from the companies building and deploying robots, and to grow a domestic component base. Today, many U.S. robot makers still rely on Chinese actuators, motors and magnets, so the near-term cost lands on them too.
Q: What has been the effect of these policy changes on companies that use or sell robotics?
A: We're seeing the issue become much more strategic. For companies deploying robotics, they are wondering more and more what their supply chain looks like five or ten years from now. A robot might be economically attractive today, but if the company is dependent on a foreign supplier for the robot itself or for critical components, that creates a different kind of risk than the traditional capital-expenditure analysis captures.
At the same time, these policies could create an opportunity for American robotics companies, but only for those that can source domestically at competitive cost.
But I don't think the answer is to simply replace every Chinese robot with an American robot. The economics have to work and companies that ultimately win will be the ones that can combine competitive economics, reliable performance and trusted supply chains. That is one reason we're paying so much attention to the companies building the underlying infrastructure and technologies that will enable the next generation of physical AI.
Q: How can companies interested in importing robotics from China best navigate the current environment?
A:  The first thing companies should do is stop treating this purely as a procurement decision. They need to look at the entire technology and supply chain stack. That means understanding exactly what they're importing, how it is classified, what tariffs and restrictions apply, where the critical components originate, what data the system collects, how the robot connects to a network, and whether there are potential national security or cybersecurity concerns.
And so, I think we need to start with the basics. Is the model already FCC authorized? Is it a mobile robot or a fixed arm? What's the duty stack on each major component? And what happens to spare parts and software updates if that supplier gets restricted?
They should also be scenario planning. What happens if the tariff changes? What happens if a particular supplier or component becomes restricted? What happens if a customer decides it cannot deploy a particular foreign-made system? Companies should build that risk analysis into their robotics strategy before they make a large deployment.
Q: Does the current policy environment change how you think about investing in robotics?
A: Absolutely, but perhaps not in the way people might expect. We don't invest in robotics simply because something is being made in the United States, and we don't avoid a company simply because it has some exposure to China. We're looking at the underlying technology, the market, the founding team, the economics and the company's ability to build a durable competitive advantage.
What has changed is that geopolitical and supply chain risk has become part of the investment thesis. When we evaluate a robotics company today, we're asking questions that weren't nearly as prominent several years ago. For example, where are the critical components coming from? Can the company manufacture at scale? How dependent is it on a particular geography? What happens if trade policy changes? Can customers deploy its technology in sensitive environments?
That's actually one of the things that makes robotics so interesting as an investment category. It’s an area that is becoming increasingly important to both economic competitiveness and national security.
Q: Everyone is talking about humanoid robots and physical AI. Beyond the hype, where are you actually seeing the most meaningful commercial traction?
A: To us, form follows function. Historically, we’ve built machines with a specific need in mind - usually to address something that humans either can't or won't do. Whether or not they resemble us wasn’t a consideration. Humanoids dominate the conversation now because they're easy to picture and designed for a world built for humans. But behind the headlines, we've seen very few verified deployments at scale.
The real traction is in purpose-built robots doing work that's dangerous, repetitive or hard for people to do consistently. That spans logistics, manufacturing, defense, healthcare, and more. What these markets share matters more than any one of them: an expensive problem, a customer who buys again after the pilot, and a clear economic outcome.
Q: What do you think investors and the broader market are still getting wrong about robotics?
A: I think there are two opposite mistakes happening at the same time. On one side, there is a tendency to underestimate robotics because people think of robots as expensive industrial machines with relatively narrow capabilities. On the other side, there is a tendency to overestimate how quickly AI will translate into fully autonomous physical systems.
 The opportunity is somewhere in between. We're entering a period where advances in AI, sensing, computation and robotics are allowing machines to operate in increasingly complex environments. But commercialization still requires solving very difficult problems around reliability, safety, manufacturing, unit economics and deployment.
That's why we believe the most interesting robotics companies aren't necessarily the ones making the biggest promises. They're the ones quietly solving difficult technical problems and demonstrating that customers are willing to pay for the result. That's ultimately what we look for as investors: not just impressive technology, but companies that can become important businesses.

articles.title: How has the cost of living changed in France, Italy, Spain and Portugal? - Al Jazeera
articles.summary: How has the cost of living changed in France, Italy, Spain and Portugal?  Al JazeeraFrom France to Albania, social unrest is setting Europe’s streets ablaze  AP NewsWhy are people protesting across Europe?  The GuardianWhat is behind the breakdown in Western society  ABC News & Headlines – Australian Broadcasting CorporationViolent protests multiply across Europe  Financial Times
articles.full_text:
Student protests in France are into their second month, escalating into demonstrations across Europe.
What began in September in France with pupils protesting against overcrowded classrooms and teacher shortages has grown into wider anger at the cost of living and planned cuts to public services.
Protesters in Albania, Belgium, Greece, Italy, Portugal and Spain have also taken to the streets over the lack of affordable housing, rising costs and failing public services – with many young people saying they no longer expect to be better off than their parents.
Facing their anger are leaders such as French President Emmanuel Macron, Italy’s Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, Spain’s PM Pedro Sanchez and Portugal’s PM Luis Montenegro. Sanchez belongs to the left, Meloni to the right and Macron and Montenegro are conservative-leaning centrists. But while their politics vary, they all face mounting unrest because of soaring costs of living.
Are they out of touch with the experiences and sentiments of youth in their countries? Al Jazeera visualises how prices, wages, housing and education have changed in France, Italy, Spain and Portugal over the past 26 years, from when Macron, Meloni, Sanchez and Montenegro were in their 20s, much like many of the protesters angry with them.
How much more expensive is it compared to 2000?
The prices paid for everyday items such as food, energy, transport and bills have risen by between 59 and 78 percent since 2000 in France, Italy, Spain and Portugal, according to Eurostat – the European Union’s statistics agency. Its harmonised index of consumer prices (HICP) is the EU’s official measure of how much everyday goods and services cost.
Spain recorded the steepest increase at 78 percent, followed by Portugal at 71 percent, 68 percent in Italy and France at 59 percent.
That means goods and services that cost 100 euros ($112) in 2000 now cost about 178 euros ($200) in Spain, 171 euros ($192) in Portugal, 168 euros ($188) in Italy and 159 euros ($178) in France.
Prices rose by about 2 percent a year on average, but jumped in 2022, when annual inflation hit 8.7 percent in Italy, 8.3 percent in Spain, 8.1 percent in Portugal and 5.9 percent in France, the highest rate in all four countries since at least 2000.
The surge was driven mainly by energy costs, which soared after Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. By October that year, eight months into the war, energy prices across the eurozone were almost 42 percent higher than a year earlier, and food prices were also rising sharply, according to Eurostat.
Between 2021 and 2023, prices increased by 12 to 15 per cent in the four countries. Wages failed to keep up, and because prices do not fall back once inflation eases, many households are still feeling the squeeze today.
How have salaries changed?
Once inflation is taken into account, the average full-time wage in Italy fell by almost 5 per cent between 2000 and 2025. Over the same period, real wages rose by 7 per cent in Spain, 11 per cent in France and 20 per cent in Portugal, according to OECD wage data adjusted with Eurostat’s price index.
In Spain most new jobs were in tourism and services, and were often seasonal and poorly paid, Jaime Velazquez, a journalist in Madrid, told Al Jazeera’s Inside Story.
Julius Fintelmann, cofounder and editor-in-chief of The European Correspondent, said ageing societies were squeezing out opportunities for younger workers, adding that the pay gap between older and younger workers has been widening across high-income economies for decades, so the promise that each generation would be better off than the last no longer holds.
How has the cost of housing changed?
Housing has become harder to afford in all four countries since 2000, according to the OECD’s price-to-income ratio. It provides a broad picture of how house prices have changed relative to incomes over time. When prices rise faster than incomes, the ratio goes up, suggesting homes are becoming less affordable on average.
However, it doesn’t show which households or regions are hit hardest, does not account for mortgage and borrowing costs, and says nothing about the quality of the homes people are paying for.
Spain has seen the biggest change. Its price-to-income ratio is 56 per cent higher than in 2000, even after falling sharply following the 2008 financial crisis.
In France, the ratio is 39 per cent higher than in 2000, though it has eased slightly since peaking in 2022.
Italy is the exception where house prices have broadly kept pace with incomes, leaving the ratio just 5 per cent higher than in 2000.
Portugal has seen the sharpest change in recent years. Its price-to-income ratio fell steadily for 15 years after 2000, meaning homes became more affordable. But since 2015 the ratio has risen by 67 per cent.
The OECD publishes the price-to-income ratio with 2015 as its reference year. To compare it with the wage and price data in this article, which started in 2000, Al Jazeera has reset the figures so that 2000 = 100.
How has state expenditure on education changed?
Education has been at the heart of the unrest in France, where protests began because of overcrowded classrooms and teacher shortages. While in Belgium and Albania, demonstrators have rallied against the rising cost of education and access to universities.
According to the latest data from Eurostat, France’s public spending on education amounts to 5.1 per cent of its gross domestic product (GDP) compared to 5.6 per cent in 2000.
Italy spent 4.4 per cent of its GDP on education compared to 4 per cent in 2024, Spain spent 4.1 per cent in 2000 and the same in 2024. Portugal spent 4.8 per cent in 2000 and 4.3 per cent in 2024.

New Delhi [India], October 19 (ANI): Union Commerce and Industry Minister Piyush Goyal on Monday said New Zealand's commitment to facilitate USD 20 billion in investments into India under the bilateral Free Trade Agreement (FTA) would strengthen manufacturing, infrastructure and services while creating new employment opportunities.
The Minister's remarks came ahead of the implementation of the India-New Zealand FTA on October 20, which will provide duty-free access to all Indian exports entering the New Zealand market.
Highlighting the investment potential of the agreement, Goyal said in a post on X, 'New Zealand's commitment to facilitate USD 20 billion in investment into India holds immense potential to strengthen manufacturing, infrastructure, services & innovation, supporting enterprise & employment.'
The investment commitment is a significant component of the agreement, which seeks to deepen economic ties between the two countries beyond trade in goods and services.
Speaking to reporters on the sidelines of an event marking the implementation of the FTA, Goyal said the agreement would benefit Indian farmers, micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs), entrepreneurs and workers across sectors.
'Starting tomorrow, 100% of the goods from every sector in India going to New Zealand will go there with zero duty,' he said.
The duty-free access is expected to improve the competitiveness of Indian exports, particularly in labour-intensive sectors such as textiles, apparel, leather and footwear, while creating opportunities for engineering goods, pharmaceuticals and agricultural products.
Goyal also highlighted the benefits for Indian farmers through a special agricultural partnership aimed at improving productivity and incomes.
'Our farmers will gain wider market access for fruits, vegetables, spices & other agricultural produce, alongside cooperation to improve productivity, support higher incomes & strengthen livelihoods,' he stated in his X post.
The Minister said Centres of Excellence would be established under the agricultural partnership, particularly in areas such as apples, kiwifruit and honey.
He also emphasised that sensitive agricultural sectors, including dairy, would remain protected under the agreement.
Goyal said the Commerce and Industry departments would work with state governments to inform farmers, entrepreneurs and businesses about opportunities arising from the FTA.
The agreement was signed on April 27 and ratified on September 21. Bilateral trade in goods and services currently stands at USD 2.4 billion, with both countries targeting NZD 7 billion in trade by 2030. (ANI)

JPMorgan Chase has made $5 billion in startup investments in the first year of its U.S. security and resiliency initiative, the company said Monday, a faster-than-expected pace that indicates the bank is finding plentiful opportunities in emerging defense, manufacturing and supply chain firms.
The bank, which last year said it would deploy $10 billion into startups over a decade, may expand the program beyond that initial dollar amount, JPMorgan co-President Doug Petno told CNBC in an interview.
Todd Combs, the former Berkshire Hathaway executive who leads the JPMorgan group in charge of making startup investments, has “hit the ground running,” Petno said. “He’s done a great job and put us in some really interesting companies,” he added.
Most of those investments have yet to be disclosed, but two known stakes seem emblematic of the project’s mission to bolster companies that are needed for a more dangerous and chaotic era of geopolitics. JPMorgan, the biggest U.S. bank by assets, has taken direct stakes in defense-related startups Hadrian and Castelion.
Wars in Ukraine and the Middle East, as well as trade disputes with China, have threatened the flow of energy and key components needed for U.S. industries and defense, which spurred JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon into creating the initiative a year ago.
He put Petno, widely seen as one of two key possible successors, in charge of the overall investment project. Combs, a former board member of the bank, reports directly to Dimon.
The scope of the project extends beyond supply chain, defense and manufacturing to include frontier technologies and the pharmaceutical and health-tech industries.
“There’s a lot of really interesting companies that have been working to solve some of these problems,” Petno said.
These “early venture-stage, advanced manufacturing companies have found ways to build these capabilities in the U.S.” rather than relying on overseas trading partners, he said.
In August, the bank helped lead a $1.4 billion funding round for Hadrian, which builds automated factories that make parts for the defense, aerospace and maritime sectors. A California factory run by Hadrian has 10 robots for every human employee, according to the startup’s founder.
That month, JPMorgan was also involved in a $1 billion funding round for Castelion, whose flagship product is a relatively low-cost hypersonic missile called Blackbeard. Castelion was founded in late 2022 by a group of former SpaceX engineers.
“Our approach is to find generational companies and partner with them for the long term,” Combs said in a statement Monday.
“Putting more than $5 billion to work in our first year shows how many exceptional businesses are building in industries that strengthen critical supply chains,” Combs said.
JPMorgan making billions of dollars of direct investments in nascent companies is a departure from its usual role as a lender and advisor.
Before the defense initiative, the bank had moved away from taking startup stakes, which can be relatively risky bets on unproven technologies. JPMorgan spun off its private equity business, One Equity Partners, more than a decade ago.
In its more traditional role, JPMorgan has also financed and facilitated more than $230 billion for industries that support American national interests, according to the bank.
That part of its security and resiliency project, meant to hit $1.5 trillion over 10 years, is led by Jay Horine, a former co-head of investment banking.
JPMorgan built a team for the project of about three dozen bankers, who are aided by hundreds more across the firm, as it expanded the initiative to Europe and Canada.
Its bankers are mapping distribution lines for key products, from submarines and missiles to aircraft, to identify suppliers that may lack the capital or capacity to meet rising demand, according to Petno.
JPMorgan is also in regular communication with the U.S. Department of Defense and Department of Commerce about the government’s needs, he said.

articles.title: Global Coalition of Fresh Produce: The Resilient Supply Chain: Collaborating to Safeguard Produce from Cyberspace to Cargo Holds - Perishable News
articles.summary: Global Coalition of Fresh Produce: The Resilient Supply Chain: Collaborating to Safeguard Produce from Cyberspace to Cargo Holds  Perishable News
articles.full_text:
October 19, 2026 | 6 min to read
Global Coalition of Fresh Produce Highlights Strategies for Building More Resilient Supply Chains
MADRID — What happens when shipping disruptions delay fresh produce shipments, leaving perishable goods stranded and at risk of waste? What if a trusted transport company turns out to be fraudulent, or a routine email contains a fake payment request?
Fresh produce businesses increasingly face multiple, concurrent challenges as they work to protect product quality, minimize losses and maintain business relationships across complex global supply chains.
These issues took center stage at The Resilient Supply Chain: Collaborating to Safeguard Produce, From Cyberspace to Cargo Holds, a speaker event organized by the Global Coalition of Fresh Produce at Fruit Attraction 2026 in Madrid. Industry experts explored how collaboration, greater transparency and stronger security practices can help protect products and build more resilient supply chains from farm to market.
The program featured keynote speaker Greg Palmer of the Canadian Produce Marketing Association (CPMA) and the Global Coalition of Fresh Produce, along with Mike Laws of Laws Logistics and the International Fresh Produce Association, Drew Zabrocki of Totem Ltd., Steve Alaerts of Foodcareplus, and Ellen Pay of the Global Coalition of Fresh Produce.
Diversified Sourcing and Flexible Logistics
In his keynote address, Palmer highlighted how changing growing conditions and market requirements are increasing the need for flexible sourcing and stronger connections between buyers and alternative production regions. Diversifying sourcing locations can create new opportunities, but it also increases the importance of reliable logistics, timely information and coordination among supply chain partners.
Rising demand and the need to protect highly perishable products are putting additional pressure on the industry to move shipments faster and more frequently. Palmer emphasized the importance of efficient shipping routes, seasonal planning and investment in port and road infrastructure.
“These trends underline the need for a more responsive supply chain—one that can adapt to changing production conditions, shipping disruptions, and market demands while protecting product quality and reducing waste,” Palmer said.
Three Doors, One Shared Vulnerability
Flexible logistics alone cannot guarantee resilience. In his presentation, Three Doors In: Security, Fraud, and the Trust Layer Fresh Produce Has to Build Together, Zabrocki examined the growing vulnerability of supply chains to cyberattacks, cargo theft and fraudulent information.
Drawing on real-world cases, he outlined three potential points of failure: vulnerabilities in shared software, criminals impersonating legitimate transport operators, and falsified documents, including fraudulent origin paperwork and payment requests. A familiar email address, convincing certificate of origin or seemingly legitimate invoice may not tell the whole story.
Zabrocki noted that businesses often lack independent ways to verify claims made by their partners.
“Because these relationships extend across the entire industry, no single company can solve the problem alone,” he said.
He recommended several practical safeguards, including understanding dependencies on third-party software, maintaining and testing backups, verifying carriers using independently sourced contact information, and confirming payment changes through separate communication channels.
Zabrocki also called for a shared, independently verifiable foundation of trust supported by common standards and open, community-owned tools. He highlighted a proposed precompetitive working group under COSSAF—the Collaboratory for Open Software & Services in Ag and Food—as a potential avenue for industry collaboration.
Laws and Alaerts echoed Zabrocki’s concerns, emphasizing that cybersecurity is becoming increasingly critical for the fresh produce industry. They stressed the need for secure, robust systems connecting supply chain operators to protect data, prevent fraud and preserve the trust that underpins reliable business relationships.
A Shared Charter for Resilient Supply Chains
How can the fresh produce industry reduce delays, prevent waste and build more resilient global supply chains? For Pay, disruption is an unavoidable reality of global trade, but its impact can be reduced through better preparation and collaboration.
“We cannot prevent every disruption, but we can prepare for it better. Through proactive planning, greater coordination, and stronger responses when challenges arise, we can build supply chains that are more stable and more resilient,” Pay said.
To support that goal, Pay presented the Global Coalition of Fresh Produce’s Charter of Good Shipping Practices, a voluntary initiative designed to provide a shared framework for more transparent, efficient and fair logistics.
The Charter is built around five guiding principles:
- Collaboration and communication
- Fair and transparent business terms
- Competition and efficiency
- Cargo integrity and product quality
- Resilience and risk preparedness
Together, these principles address practical challenges facing fresh produce businesses, including the need for timely information, clearer commercial terms, fairer sharing of costs and risks, and logistics practices that protect the quality and value of perishable goods. Better coordination can help businesses respond to disruptions, avoid unnecessary inefficiencies and reduce food waste.
Pay stressed that the Charter is not intended to impose new rules, but to establish a common reference point for the industry.
“This is not about one player versus another,” she said. “It is about the supply chain we all share. If we can build greater transparency, fairness, and efficiency into our relationships, we can create a system that is stronger and more sustainable for everyone.”
Pay concluded by encouraging businesses and industry associations to contribute to the Charter’s development and help make it a practical tool for the entire supply chain.
Building Resilience Together
Discussions at Fruit Attraction highlighted the interconnected nature of the industry’s challenges. Climate disruptions are changing where produce can be sourced, evolving markets are demanding faster and more flexible transportation, and growing digital and commercial risks are making trust and verification essential.
No company can build a resilient supply chain alone. Progress depends on cooperation among growers, exporters, logistics providers, buyers and industry organizations, supported by shared standards, reliable information and practical safeguards.
The Global Coalition of Fresh Produce’s Charter of Good Shipping Practices offers a voluntary framework for turning that shared commitment into action through better communication, fairer business practices and stronger risk preparedness.
Put the Charter Into Practice
The Global Coalition of Fresh Produce invites stakeholders across the global fresh produce supply chain to support the Charter of Good Shipping Practices and apply its principles in their day-to-day operations.
By embracing the Charter, organizations can help foster greater transparency, fairness and collaboration; improve logistics efficiency; reduce avoidable waste; and strengthen supply chain resilience.
Participation also demonstrates a commitment to transparency and environmental stewardship while supporting more efficient, fair and sustainable logistics. Collaborative practices can streamline operations, optimize resource use and reduce waste, delivering lasting financial benefits.
The Charter and a summary are available through the Global Coalition of Fresh Produce. To learn more or express support, contact the coalition’s secretariat at info@producecoalition.net.

Thai Trade Representative Werapong Prapha has asked the Netherlands to support better European Union (EU) market access for white rice, chicken and canned tuna, as both countries back efforts to conclude Thailand–EU free trade negotiations by the end of 2026.
Werapong discussed the proposed free trade agreement (FTA) with Sjoerd Sjoerdsma, the Netherlands’ Minister of Foreign Trade and Development Cooperation, at the Dutch Embassy in Thailand. The talks also covered the direction of economic cooperation and the global trading environment.
Thailand’s request for support from the Netherlands, an important EU member, is intended to secure market-opening terms that deliver tangible benefits for Thai businesses and the public, Werapong said.
Thailand and the Netherlands supported accelerating the FTA negotiations towards a conclusion in 2026, while balancing speed with the quality of the agreement and building acceptance among the sectors affected, according to Werapong.
The Thai–Dutch discussions also examined the balance between opening agricultural and industrial goods markets. Werapong emphasised the importance of concrete outcomes acceptable to all sectors.
The Netherlands raised concerns about industrial policy and trade competition during the discussions, Werapong said. Those issues are important to both the Dutch side and the wider EU.
Following the ministerial talks, Werapong exchanged views with Thai and Dutch business representatives attending the opening of the Dutch Embassy’s new premises in Thailand.
Businesses represented at the embassy opening included FrieslandCampina (Foremost), East-West Seed, Signify, KLM Royal Dutch Airlines, Central Group, Indorama Ventures, Siam Cement Group (SCG) and Thai Union.
Thailand used the business discussions to emphasise its ambition to be a mutually supportive and dependable trading partner, Werapong said. The Thai side also outlined efforts to drive economic growth through structural reforms and promote more transparent and predictable trade rules.
Thailand’s approach to attracting investment focuses on priority areas including advanced technology, medical tourism, electric vehicles, upgrading agricultural and food value chains, and clean energy, according to Werapong.
The Netherlands is Thailand’s 19th-largest trading partner worldwide and its second-largest within the EU. Bilateral trade totalled US$7,967.56 million in 2025, accounting for 1.16% of Thailand’s total trade.
Thai exports to the Netherlands amounted to US$7,019.53 million in 2025, while imports from the Netherlands totalled US$948.03 million.
Thailand’s main exports to the Netherlands included computers and related equipment and components, electrical transformers and components, other electrical appliances and components, integrated circuits, and meat and edible offal.
Thailand’s principal imports from the Netherlands included integrated circuits, machinery and components, chemicals, medical and pharmaceutical products, and scientific and medical instruments and equipment.

articles.title: Malaysia’s exports hit five-year high in September as electronics shipments jump - KLSE Screener
articles.summary: Malaysia’s exports hit five-year high in September as electronics shipments jump  KLSE Screener
articles.full_text:
KUALA LUMPUR (Oct 19): Malaysian exports rose to its highest in five years in September as electronics shipments expanded sharply while orders from key markets like the US and China soared.
Exports totalled RM215.1 billion, an increase of 54.5% year-on-year, according to data released by the Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry (Miti) on Monday. The expansion exceeded the median forecast of 39.9% in a Bloomberg survey and accelerated from August’s 45.5% growth.
“Malaysia’s trade performance remains exposed to uncertainties arising from shifting trade policies by major economies and geopolitical tensions,” the ministry said.
The ongoing conflicts in West Asia, in particular, could disrupt global trade flows and intensify cost pressures, Miti said, adding that it will continue to “assess these developments, strengthen market diversification, expand access to high-growth markets and help Malaysian exporters adapt”.
Electrical and electronics, which accounted for more than half of the total exports, jumped 68% and reported a new monthly record high. Optical and scientific equipment, such as specialised medical gear and semiconductor test instruments, also reported their highest monthly export value.
Exports of petroleum products climbed 33% while liquefied natural gas surged 46%.
By destination, exports to the US recorded a 72% gain while deliveries to China, the biggest trading partner of Malaysia, were 52% higher. Shipments to Taiwan and South Korea both more than doubled.
Imports, meanwhile, climbed 52.7% to RM181.4 billion in September, also exceeding the Bloomberg survey’s forecast of 39% growth.
By end use, imports of intermediate goods — semi-finished goods used in final assembly of products such as computers or cars — climbed 69.6% to RM92.1 billion. Capital goods imports increased 20.9% while consumption goods rose 18.2%.
All in all, Malaysia reported a trade surplus of RM33.7 billion in September, widening 65% year-on-year and 20% month-on-month.

articles.title: Australian super funds on precipice of strategic tilt towards Asia - AFR
articles.summary: Australian super funds on precipice of strategic tilt towards Asia  AFR
articles.full_text:
“Asia’s relative economic strengths and the opportunities to diversify along the supply chain and into high growth sectors have become more appealing. We are seeing a structural strategic tilt towards Asia.”
Australian super funds already have exposure to Asian markets, but growing concentration risk elsewhere in their portfolios is prompting closer consideration of the region’s role in their global allocations.
Morningstar Research indicates geopolitics has become a more prominent factor for Asia Pacific investors, including Australian super funds, than for asset owners in other jurisdictions.
Its 2026 Asset Owner Perspectives Survey shows more investors in the Asia Pacific region (82 per cent) than Europe (74 per cent) and North America (68 per cent) are focused on geopolitics.
Asia’s growth advantage
Asia’s economic outlook offers Australian super funds exposure to growth forecasted to outpace the global economy.
HSBC Global Investment Research indicates that GDP across Asia will grow by 4.2 per cent in 2026 and by 4.1 per cent in 2027, exceeding anticipated global GDP growth of 2.5 per cent in 2026 and 2.7 per cent in 2027.
This economic growth is leading to demographic shifts. Data shows the middle class is expected to comprise 70 per cent of ASEAN’s population by 2030, boosting demand for consumer products and services, and leading to development of new trade and service capabilities across the region.
That expansion will also increase demand for infrastructure and utilities. Transport networks, energy systems and digital infrastructure will need to support growing populations and businesses, creating potential long-term investment opportunities for institutional investors.
“Asia is a powerful engine of global growth, backed by diversified, efficient supply chains with a growing middle-class consumer market,” says Danielle Johnson, global head of institutional client group, HSBC.
“As geopolitics reshape global trade corridors, Asia’s economies are well positioned to capture a bigger share of these trade flows, marking a growing opportunity for institutional investors to de-risk and diversify across markets.”
Much of the boost to Asian economic growth is expected to come from rapid expansion across the AI, semiconductor and robotics sectors. Investment in new digital and urban infrastructure will add to productivity.
World Economic Forum figures show the ASEAN digital economy, presently valued at around $US300 billion, is forecast to reach $US1 trillion by 2030.
Successful implementation of the ASEAN Digital Economy Framework Agreement (DEFA) could potentially double this to $US2 trillion. The Australian super sector could share in this growth, but expertise is required to pick the right assets.
Local insight reduces risk
In the past, superannuation funds have taken a measured approach to increasing their exposure to Asian markets, given shifting market dynamics across these jurisdictions. As concentration risk encourages funds to broaden their geographic allocations, geopolitical risk and market volatility remain factors they need to manage when increasing their exposure to Asia.
Nevertheless, Asia is not monolithic; Asian nations have different laws, taxes, regulations, rules around foreign ownership, investment structures and capital protections. This can be tricky to navigate and super funds are working with partners who understand these variables.
“Entering a new market requires strong foreign exchange capabilities, custody and transaction banking infrastructure and market intelligence, informed by on-the-ground expertise. It requires a partner with a breadth of services in Australia and in the markets super funds are trying to access,” says Johnson.
Cross-border expertise
Looking ahead, expect deeper ties between Australia and Asia, with more cross-pollination between markets.
“There is a growing appreciation of the deep links that already exist and considerable bilateral investment between Australia and Asia,” says Scholfield.
Education and tourism have helped strengthen ties between Australia and Asia. According to the Australian Department of Education, 57 per cent of international students studying in Australia in the first half of 2026 came from five countries across Asia, including China, India and Vietnam.
“This familiarity is enormously positive and will continue to open doors between the jurisdictions, thanks to a workforce with ties to both regions,” says Johnson.

KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia's external trade in September 2026 hit a fresh milestone with total trade expanding 53.7% year-on-year (y-o-y) to RM396.5bil, according to the Ministry of Investment, Trade and Industry (Miti).
It capped off nine months of trade growth, with total trade rising 30.1% y-o-y to RM2.91 trillion. Exports from January to September rose 34% to RM1.571 trillion while imports expanded 25.7% to RM1.339 trillion. The trade surplus widened 115.7% to RM232.38bil.
In September, exports soared 54.5% to RM215.11bil, while imports rose 52.7% to RM181.39bil. The trade surplus came to RM33.72bil, representing the 77th consecutive month of surplus since May 2020.
By trade destination, major trading partners Asean, China and the US, all received higher shipments of goods from Malaysia.
Total exports to Asean surged 46.2% to RM59.55bil, supported by strong exports of E&E products as well as machinery, equipment and parts.
Exports to China increased 22.1% to RM20.39 bil, marking the ninth successive month of expansion, boosted by strong exports of E&E products, LNG as well as metalliferous ores and metal scrap.
For the US, an increase in E&E exports took total outbound shipments 89.9% higher to a record RM38.03bil.
Miti said the outlook for Malaysia's trade remained positive but the trade performance remained exposed to uncertainties arising from shifting trade policies by major economies and geopolitical tensions. In particular, the ongoing conflicts in West Asia could disrupt global trade flows and intensify cost pressures.
"Miti and Matrade will continue to assess these developments, strengthen market diversification, expand access to high-growth markets and help Malaysian exporters adapt to evolving global trade conditions," Miti said in a statement.
Exports of manufactured goods in September surged 58.6% y-o-y to a record high of RM191.57bil, underpinned by rising exports of E&E products, petroleum products, optical and scientific equipment as well as machinery, equipment and parts.
Outbound shipments of mining goods soared 56.3% y-o-y to RM11.43bil, the highest value ever recorded, due to an increase in exports of LNG, supported by higher export prices, and crude petroleum, attributed to both higher export prices and quantities, as well as metalliferous ores and metal scrap.
Agriculture goods exports dropped 5.7% y-o-y to RM9.03bil due to a decrease in the value of palm oil and palm oil-based agriculture products due to reduced export quantity.
Meanwhile, Malaysia's imports saw a 50.8% increase in intermediate goods to RM92.1bil. Capitals good increased 20.9% y-oy to RM22.32bil and consumption goods expanded 18.2% o RM10.91bil.

Token going global is emerging as a brand new business.
On the evening of October 18, a $200 million (equivalent to 1.338 billion yuan) AI order has placed Runjian Co., Ltd. in the spotlight of Token offshore business.
This A-share company, whose main business covers communication network management, operation and maintenance and has been continuously laying out computing power services in recent years, has just obtained a cross-border AI service contract worth 200 million US dollars. The contract has a term of one year, overseas customers call large model inference services through API interfaces, and all relevant computing power resources are deployed in intelligent computing centers within China's territory.
More notably, the contract includes a minimum purchase guarantee clause: if the service fee corresponding to the Token actually consumed by the customer during the contract year is less than 200 million US dollars, the difference shall be made up as agreed.
The amount of this single order is equivalent to about 35.6% of Runjian Co., Ltd.'s operating revenue in the first half of 2026. What it sells is neither servers nor chips, and what customers purchase is the Token consumed during the operation of the large model.
A new profit-making model is emerging in China's AI offshore business: converting domestic computing power resources into services, allowing overseas customers to call them via the network and pay according to usage.
This transaction also brings a concept that originally mostly appeared in AI industry discussions into the commercial contracts of listed companies.
In the past, when the market paid attention to China's AI going global, it usually focused on whether large models could catch up with overseas competitors and whether domestic chips could enter the international market. Nowadays, model invocation services, inference computing power and Token billing have also become new directions for enterprises to explore overseas revenue.
For China's AI industry chain, this means new market space. For Runjian Co., Ltd., a large contract also brings a more realistic test question: when the intelligent computing centers built in China start to serve overseas customers, how much profit can this business really make?
After all, 200 million US dollars is only the contract amount. What really determines the value of this transaction also includes computing power cost, equipment depreciation, customer payment collection, and whether service providers can retain sufficient profits in the fierce price competition.
The first large order of Token offshore business has been signed. Next, the market needs to see how this business turns from contract amount to real revenue and profits.
01
China's AI Going Global Has Opened Up a New Path
To understand Token offshore business, we must first figure out what exactly customers are purchasing.
When users ask questions to large models, generate texts or write codes, the model will process the input content and generate output results. Inputs and outputs are usually measured by Token, and service providers charge fees according to model types, input and output quantities and specific billing rules.
Developers can call the model through API and integrate it into their own applications. Therefore, overseas enterprises can directly use AI capabilities without building a complete model inference system on their own.
This model reduces the initial investment for customers to use AI, and also gives model service providers the opportunity to charge by usage.
The increasing activity of Chinese large models in overseas developer communities has laid a market foundation for this business.
Chinese AI enterprises including DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, Zhipu AI, MiniMax and other Chinese AI enterprises are expanding overseas markets through different model products and technical routes. Model performance, invocation price, open weight strategy and developer tools will all affect the choices of overseas customers.
For developers, when choosing models, they often need to consider the answer quality, response speed, invocation cost and stability at the same time. As long as the model can meet specific business needs and is competitively priced, it will have the opportunity to enter application development and enterprise workflows.
However, there is still a gap between getting attention for the model and achieving commercial success. Developer trial, actual payment, enterprise procurement and long-term renewal represent market progress at different stages. The increase in invocation volume also needs to be combined with price changes and cost structure to judge the quality of revenue growth.
This order of Runjian Co., Ltd. provides another perspective for observation.
The company has long been engaged in communication network management, operation and maintenance, and has gradually expanded its digital network, energy network and computing power network businesses. With the accumulation of intelligent computing center construction and operation capabilities, the company has begun to explore new computing power services such as Token.
In this contract, Wuxiang Cloud Valley provides large model inference invocation services to overseas customers through API, and the computing power facilities remain in China. Customers can use relevant resources remotely and settle accounts in accordance with the contract agreement.
This kind of business arrangement provides a feasible path for China's computing power infrastructure to participate in the global AI market. Even if enterprises do not independently develop basic models, they can still participate in this market by virtue of their computing power resources, technical operation and service delivery capabilities.
02
Competition Lies in Price, Computing Power and Payment Collection
In the Token industry chain, there are at least two types of enterprises looking for commercial opportunities.
The first type is model vendors. They provide API services of self-developed models to customers, and their revenue is related to customer invocation volume, product pricing and contract arrangements. The model's capabilities, inference efficiency and developer ecosystem determine whether enterprises can continuously attract customers.
The second type is computing power service providers. They provide services around computing resources, inference deployment, API access and operation delivery. Some enterprises have their own intelligent computing centers, while others provide services by integrating computing resources from different sources.
The contract of Runjian Co., Ltd. this time is closer to the latter model.
The capability requirements for the two types of enterprises are different. Model vendors need to continuously improve model performance and control the cost of each inference; computing power service providers need to do a good job in resource scheduling, equipment maintenance and customer service, so as to obtain higher utilization rate of existing computing resources.
The two sides can also form a cooperative relationship. Models, computing power, interface services and overseas customer channels can be provided by different enterprises respectively, and then connected through commercial contracts.
This division of labor expands the space for China's AI industry chain to participate in the overseas market, and also brings new competition.
When more and more enterprises can provide similar inference services, customers will compare invocation prices, response speed, service stability and technical support capabilities. If service providers lack obvious cost advantages or customer stickiness, revenue growth will easily be affected by price competition.
Therefore, Token invocation volume is only one indicator to measure business scale. Customer retention rate, single inference cost, service gross profit margin and payment collection situation also determine the value of this business.
03
How Much Profit Can It Bring to Runjian Co., Ltd.?
The scale of this contract of Runjian Co., Ltd. is quite considerable.
The company achieved an operating revenue of 3.756 billion yuan in the first half of 2026, and the contract amount of 200 million US dollars is equivalent to about 35.6% of its operating revenue in the first half of the year.
However, there are obvious differences between contract amount, current period revenue and profit.
According to the announcement, the contract term is from October 19, 2026 to October 18, 2027, the service adopts the post-payment mode by usage, and the settlement cycle is a natural month. The finally confirmed revenue amount needs to be determined according to actual performance and accounting treatment.
The contract also sets an annual minimum purchase guarantee clause. If the service fee corresponding to the Token actually consumed by the customer during the contract year is less than 200 million US dollars, the difference shall be made up as agreed. This provides certain purchase guarantee for the contract, but customer payment, contract performance and revenue confirmation still need subsequent verification.
The profit performance of Runjian Co., Ltd.'s existing computing power business can also help understand the cost pressure faced by this order.
According to the company's 2026 semi-annual report, the computing power network business achieved an operating revenue of about 519 million yuan in the first half of the year, a year-on-year increase of 50.31%; the operating cost was about 483 million yuan, a year-on-year increase of 55.08%; the gross profit margin was 6.97%, down 2.86 percentage points year-on-year.
Revenue is growing rapidly, while the cost is growing even faster. The company stated that the low gross profit margin of the Token factory business is mainly affected by factors such as high depreciation during the period of fixed assets put into operation.

articles.title: We must tax the wealth of billionaires, not just income. California can lead the way | Ro Khanna
articles.summary: Will California stand with the working class or the oligarchs in the vote this November?The Democratic party has a choice to make. Are we going to be New Deal Democrats or corporate Democrats? Are we standing with the working class or the tech oligarchs?Proposition 40, California’s billionaire tax, is the most important ballot initiative in America and a fight for the soul of our party.Rohit Khanna is aUS congressman and attorney serving as the US representative from California’s 17th congressio...
articles.full_text:
The Democratic party has a choice to make. Are we going to be New Deal Democrats or corporate Democrats? Are we standing with the working class or the tech oligarchs?
Proposition 40, California’s billionaire tax, is the most important ballot initiative in America and a fight for the soul of our party.
Senator Bernie Sanders and I stand with the nurses and healthcare workers who put Prop 40 on the ballot. Governor Gavin Newsom stands with Peter Thiel, Sergey Brin and Elon Musk, Trump backers who all oppose it.
Prop 40 is a one-time 5% tax on the roughly 250 billionaires who live in the state. Together they hold wealth equal to half of California’s economy. That wealth is up 20% this year alone.
If they paid this tax, they would be worth the same as they were on Labor Day of this year. That’s the speed at which their wealth is growing. The tax would raise about $100bn, 90% of it for healthcare. It would help keep 3 million Californians from losing coverage. Trump’s cuts could cost Medi-Cal more than $30bn a year, and this tax would help fill that gigantic hole.
Thiel, Brin and Musk have all funded Trump and his party. Thiel gave $1.25m to elect Trump in 2016. Brin gave nearly $500,000 to the Republican National Committee last year. Musk spent roughly $290m to help return Trump to power. On 8 October, Trump awarded Brin and Musk the National Medal of Science.
Brin has spent $102m to kill Prop 40. Thiel gave $3m to block it. Musk attacked it on X, warning that “they will eventually apply the ‘wealth tax’ to everyone”. The day after Trump’s ceremony, Newsom endorsed Prop 42, Brin’s measure to cancel it.
Billionaires have outspent Prop 40’s supporters more than five to one. Musk has given $366n to federal campaigns in this election cycle alone.
Tax billionaires so they can’t buy democracy.
I have made my choice. I endorsed Prop 40, and I will vote no on Prop 42. The California Democratic party took the same positions in August. The governor has made the opposite choice on both.
He fought to keep Prop 40 off the ballot. When the healthcare workers behind it offered to cut the rate to 2% if he would back it, he said no. Now the No on 40 campaign features him in its ads.
Most cynically, Newsom has become the poster child for Prop 42, a billionaire-written provision, which would ban California from ever taxing billionaire wealth.
He will sadly be more remembered for trying to tank Prop 40 (taxing billionaires) than helping pass Prop 50 (redistricting).
Bernie and I believe the fight doesn’t stop with Prop 40. In March, we introduced the Make Billionaires Pay Their Fair Share Act, a 5% annual tax on America’s 938 billionaires, worth $8.2tn.
It would raise more than $4tn over a decade, enough to reverse Trump’s $1.1tn in healthcare cuts, send $12,000 to every family of four making $150,000 or less, and fund free childcare and free college.
I am with the working class.
In 1911, Wisconsin pioneered the income tax because a property tax on land was no longer enough once industry was producing most of the wealth. Two years later, the country adopted the 16th amendment.
Today, California is pioneering a billionaire tax for an economy where explosive asset appreciation escapes ordinary taxation. If voters pass Prop 40, California will be the first place to figure out how to tax billionaire wealth, setting a model for the nation and the world.
For too long, our party has answered to corporate donors before workers. The factory towns and rural counties our governing class ignored stopped believing us. Trump promised to fight for them, then cut taxes for billionaires and cut Medicaid. We will not win those voters back by protecting the same billionaires in Sacramento. You cannot oppose the Trump administration while doing the bidding of its donors.
Anyone who wants to lead this party has to say where they stand on Prop 40.
Every society is taxed. The only question is who will pay. In Trump’s America, working people pay more than they should, while billionaires are so unburdened that they are becoming trillionaires. In the America we seek, billionaires and trillionaires will pay their fair share, while working people will be unburdened.
Will California this November stand with the working class or the oligarchs?
- Rohit Khanna is aUS congressman and attorney serving as the US representative from California’s 17th congressional district

articles.title: No, DataCenters are Not Crowding-Out Other Investments
articles.summary:

The post No, DataCenters are Not Crowding-Out Other Investments appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.
articles.full_text:
Based on charts like the one at right, Paul Krugman and many others are arguing that:
Massive spending on data centers is crowding out investment in everything else in the economy.
Not so fast. Can you see one immediate problem? How is $51b in data center construction spending crowding out $120b in everything else!
Indeed, crowding out in the standard loanable funds model is generically less than 1 to 1–that is, $51b of additional spending will crowd out less than $51b of other investment spending. The standard analysis is that increased investment demand/borrowing increases interest rates–the higher interest rate reduces investment demand elsewhere (that’s the crowding out) but the higher interest rate also increases savings so investment elsewhere falls by less than the increase in tech investment. Here’s the classic graph from our textbook, Modern Principles. In the graph, we explain crowding out in terms of government borrowing but formally the diagram is the same with tech borrowing substituting for government borrowing:

Although the diagram is formally identical with private borrowing or government borrowing the term crowding-out is usually reserved for the latter. Private borrowing faces the market test so “crowding out” in that context simply means funds flowing from lower value to higher valued uses–it’s a benefit. Government borrowing doesn’t face the same market test and so we need to remind people that it comes at a cost. Let’s put this point aside, however.
Krugman doesn’t point out the problem with Rattner’s graph but he does substitute with a graph of his own (shown below) which compares all “tech” investment with all other investment as a share of GDP. On the surface that seems to at least get the ratios in more plausible alignment but there are a few problems. First, the numbers are on a different order of magnitude. Rattner has annual datacenter investment rising to $51b (annual rate) over a more than two year period. Krugman has tech spending rising to ~$539b over a similar period–so far more than datacenters or AI as conventionally considered is being counted. That’s fine–but Krugman is relying here on datacenter discontent while actually discussing something different. But there is another problem.

Krugman’s graph is in terms of shares of GDP and as one share is going up, another is going down which is meant to be suggestive of crowding out–except GDP is increasing. Let’s regraph the same data in dollars and in real terms:

Now the picture looks different. From 2023 Q2 to 2026 Q2, real tech investment rose about 46%, while other real investment rose about 3%. Other investment has weakened since its 2024 peak, but it remains above its starting level. This does not rule out crowding out: other investment might have grown faster without the tech boom. But we have now gone from charts suggesting that crowding out was absolute to arguing that it was relative to GDP and relative to a counter-factual which cannot be identified with these graphs.
So what is really going on? Real interest rates are up since the pandemic but most of the increase happened before the AI investment boom. The average 10-year TIPS yield rose from −1.00% in late 2021 to 1.49% in late 2022. In comparison, the increase in rates over the Rattner/Krugman chart-periods are only .5 and 0.68 percentage points respectively, relatively small potatoes to hang a crowding out story.
Moreover, current real rates are ~2-3%, in line with historical averages and hardly prohibitive. If there are good projects they can be funded.
Why did real rates rise if not datacenter borrowing? There are many possible explanations: recovery from unusually low rates during the pandemic, Federal borrowing, maybe even a quite different tech story in which greater expectations of future wealth are reducing savings today (like the reputed AI workers who have taken up smoking because they expect a future cure for lung cancer). But note that real rates are up across advanced economies, not just here, even though most of the AI spending is here–this further weakens the case for crowding out of US investment, as the world saving base is much larger than the US base.
Bottom line is that I think a more plausible story is that two things are happening at once: tariffs, uncertainty, and other forces including the fading of Biden-era CHIPS and IRA subsidies have weakened investment outside AI-tech. The AI boom in contrast has supported overall investment. In other words, rather than datacenters and AI investment “crowding out” other investment, my interpretation is that AI investment is a bright spot in what would otherwise be a more negative economy.
Hat tip: Arpit Gupta.

The post The California billionaire tax is very likely a net revenue loser appeared first on Marginal REVOLUTION.
articles.full_text:
This paper examines the revenue and migration impact of the 2026 California Billionaire Tax Act, a one-time 5 percent tax on the worldwide net worth of individuals exceeding $1 billion. Using data from the Forbes Billionaire List, news reports detailing the residential real estate holdings of California billionaires, and public announcements of billionaire departures from the state, we estimate the behavioral response and associated revenue loss to this new tax using several different methodologies. Even before accounting for reductions in other tax bases such as the income tax, we estimate that the Act will collect approximately $30 billion (range $28 to 36 billion), less than a third of the $100 billion projected by Galle et al. (2025). This range accounts for the publicly confirmed taxpayer migration that has already eliminated nearly 30 percent of the Act’s wealth tax base, applies a litigation-survival discount to the remaining base, and is validated by the wealth tax base elasticity literature. We estimate that California’s billionaires contribute $3.3–5.8 billion annually in state income taxes. The present value of permanently lost income tax collections from departures more than offsets the one-time wealth tax revenue, yielding a net present value of negative $38.9 billion. Across 100,000 simulated revenue and discount rate combinations, 85 percent of plausible outcomes produce a negative net present value of state revenues.
That is from a new NBER working paper by Benjamin Jaros and Joshua Rauh.  Overall this issue is a good litmus test for who still thinks like an economist.

articles.full_text:
An excellent and also original movie, you all should see it.  There are different interpretations, but I read it as a story between two autistic people, and the bond they have but also the great difficulties they have in understanding each other, because they are so very different.  I am not saying that is what the moviemakers intended, but I feel it is what they ended up putting on the screen.
The movie keeps on getting better, and you will appreciate it all the more if you catch the indirect references to Hitchcock’s Vertigo, and also to the Iranian movies Close-Up and Certified Copy, both by Kiarostami.
Of course Holmes should not be in jail (house arrest?), and this movie cements the view I already held.  I come away from this movie with a consistent sense of her, rather than with the feeling we can never know a person.

articles.full_text:
The author is Edward Cutler and the subtitle is How Italy’s Nature Shaped its Culture and Civilisation.  This is an excellent book on how “the Italy you know” has been shaped by its natural environment, such as its mountains, rivers, geology, and so on.  Ever wondered why Sardinia is different?  The book is good at sticking to specifics.  Excerpt:
This extraordinary overlap has made Italy the continent’s botanical crossroads and one of its greatest arboreal sanctuaries.  Within Europe, few countries host such a variety of native trees: at least 140 species, more than almost anywhere west of the Balkans.  Some, like the Sicilian fir, Lobel’s maple and the Etna birch, are totally unique.  The structure of Italy’s forests is equally diverse — dense, high-altitude canopies, open oak pastures, cork scrub and coastal maquis, each shaped by centuries of disturbance and renewal.  This is the legacy of a land that sreved first as Europe’s refuge during the Ice Ages and later as its great corridor of return, where northern, eastern and African floras met and mingled in perpetual exchange.
Recommended to all those with an interest in Italy.

articles.full_text:
What we find here is that the quality-adjusted screen time price index is down 39 per cent since 2000, but that change is overwhelmingly a function of improvements in quality, not declines in prices paid for devices, subscriptions and so on. So the steep rise in screen time over the past 20 years has led to a 52 per cent rise in real-terms spending per person on digital technology.
What seemed at first like a story of screen time outcompeting socialising and reading thanks to a widening advantage on cost, now looks more like digital technology winning out through the sheer force of unparalleled convenience and attention capture, even if that comes at a mounting financial (let alone social) cost.

articles.full_text:
Björn Öste is building Arkhub, an AI-powered platform that analyzes remote-sensing and other archaeological data to identify potential ancient sites in the Amazon and enable further investigation by citizen scientists.
J. Cameron Monroe is leading the Allada Regional Archaeology Project, using lidar, remote sensing, and archaeological fieldwork to reconstruct the historical landscape of the Kingdom of Allada and strengthen cultural heritage preservation in Benin.

Previously reported grantees include:

Benjamin Arbuckle is combining archaeology and ancient DNA analysis to reconstruct entire ecosystems of ancient cities, with the goal of understanding how human societies can thrive in balance with their environments.
Jesse Casana, an archaeology professor at Dartmouth, is developing drone-based radar imaging methods to detect and map archaeological sites buried beneath desert sands. His work combines advanced remote-sensing technologies with efforts to preserve endangered cultural landscapes.
Leila Character is developing drone-based imaging and AI tools to detect hidden archaeological sites, making discovery faster, cheaper, and more accessible to researchers worldwide.
Bryce Hoenigman is developing an AI tool to help date ancient cuneiform tablets by analyzing how written symbols evolved over time, with the goal of making archaeological research faster and more accurate.

With thanks to Yonatan Ben Shimon for his generosity in support of this.  We do still have funds remaining in this tranche…

articles.title: How Ryder Kemper became employee #7 at Corgi Insurance — and never left San Francisco
articles.summary: Ryder flew to SF for a work trial, moved furniture in a Mystery Machine bus, and decided to stay. Here's what building from day one looks like.
articles.full_text:
Ryder Kemper was in Ohio, winding down a startup he and his college friends had built together.
The team had decided to close it — not because it failed, but because they wanted different things.
Ryder knew he wanted to stay in startups, and he knew he wanted to be in San Francisco.
A message on Work at a Startup from Corgi Insurance's first sales hire changed everything.
He did a thirty-minute interview on a Friday, flew to SF on Sunday for a work trial, and never went back.
"By the time I had an offer, I had already helped to get the signature Costco mattresses into the house we were living in.
"Corgi Insurance (YC S24) is rebuilding core financial infrastructure from the ground up — insurance systems, policy administration, claims — with the goal of owning the stack end to end.
Ryder with Emily Yuan and Nico Laqua, Co-Founders of Corgi, at an early team bonfire in SF.
The Mystery Machine testRyder's work trial was not a whiteboard exercise.
He spent roughly half his time writing code and the other half riding in the company's Mystery Machine bus, hauling furniture to a new office.
That ratio told him something important about the kind of place Corgi was.
"The energy was just different.
I felt like there was a good chance of success but worst case scenario it would be a great time.
"He calls himself employee number seven.
His self-assigned title: Chief Furniture Mover.
What he actually buildsRyder has touched nearly every part of Corgi's technical stack:Core policy administration and claims systemsNew product development as Corgi launches additional insurance linesHiring processes for new engineers and teamsThe claims system is the project he talks about most.
Working closely with adjusters who "think its all magic and crazy how fast we can put stuff together," he gets fast, enthusiastic feedback that makes the next iteration easier to ship.
The loop is tight: build, get it live — sometimes before it feels fully ready — then iterate on real feedback from customers and the sales team.
His current tool of choice is Claude Code.
He recently set up a desktop at home he can shell into remotely, letting his AI agents run even when his laptop is offline.
One trick he likes: having Claude generate artifacts beyond terminal output — diagrams in Figma, recorded videos of pull-request work — to make its output more understandable to the rest of the team.
Why the people matter"The concentration of talent here is really crazy," Ryder says.
What stands out to him is the default posture: no idea is too big, no challenge gets waved off.
"The default answer is always 'yea we can do that,' or 'why don't we just do it ourselves.
'" The founders give people real freedom to operate, and Ryder says he has learned a lot about business just by watching how they navigate situations nobody on the team has seen before.
He also notes, with equal sincerity, that he was surprised by how much milk co-founder Nico can drink.
Two years, ten years of workRyder estimates he has packed about ten years' worth of experience into roughly two.
He has shifted between building, managing, and scoping new projects, but has stayed close to whatever Corgi is working on next.
"To me everything still feels like a new startup.
" He has also discovered something unexpected about himself: he is happier with less stuff.
Moving around frequently for work, he stopped accumulating things and found he didn't miss them.
He plans to start his own company one day.
For now, Corgi is the place where he is learning how.
Who would thrive hereIf you want clear boundaries and a narrow job description, this is not the role.
If you want to ship fast, own entire projects end to end, and do whatever needs doing — engineering or otherwise — Ryder's advice is simple: "Expect a lot of uncertainty but also a crazy journey that has not really been matched by anything else in my experience.
Expect to work extremely hard and constantly feel like there's never enough time for anything.
Expect to learn a lot about yourself and make a new group of close friends.
"Corgi Insurance is hiring.
You can find them on Work at a Startup.

articles.title: Christiane Amanpour announces she’s leaving CNN after 43 years
articles.summary: Anchor’s departure not thought to be linked to company’s recent acquisition by David Ellison’s Skydance MediaChristiane Amanpour, one of CNN’s most decorated and venerated journalists, is leaving the network after 43 years, she said in a statement on Monday.Amanpour, who began working for the then-fledging network as an assistant on the international assignment desk in 1983 and is now its chief international anchor, will end her show Amanpour in May and leave the network at the end of June. articles.full_text:
Christiane Amanpour, one of CNN’s most decorated and venerated journalists, is leaving the network after 43 years, she said in a statement on Monday.
Amanpour, who began working for the then-fledging network as an assistant on the international assignment desk in 1983 and is now its chief international anchor, will end her show Amanpour in May and leave the network at the end of June. She also hosts a show for PBS, Amanpour and Company, that will conclude at the end of this year.
In the statement, Amanpour said she came to the decision to “separate” from the network “after many months of thought and a few sleepless nights”.
“From my very first big exciting assignment covering the first Gulf war, to the horrors of the Bosnian war, Rwanda, Afghanistan, Ukraine and Iran and all the points in between, it’s the teams and the camaraderie that counted so much, as we together battled to seek the facts, the evidence and the humanity, so that CNN could always broadcast the truth about the world and to the world, without fear nor favor,” she wrote.
She ended her statement by encouraging her CNN colleagues: “Remember: always be truthful, not neutral.”
Amanpour, 68, has been open about her ongoing treatment for ovarian cancer, which she was diagnosed with in 2021.
Her decision comes at a notable time for the network, which is now part of a larger media conglomerate called Skydance that is run by David Ellison, with heavy backing from Larry Ellison, his Trump-donor father and Oracle co-founder.
Her exit is not thought to be specifically tied to the network’s new ownership, which is viewed skeptically by some CNN journalists because of its perceived closeness to the Trump administration. But, in her statement, Amanpour seemed to nod to concerns about the network’s future, saying that she “will always be rooting for CNN and maintaining its history of independent journalism”.
She expanded on that commitment to independence in a taped message to viewers of her CNN International show on Monday afternoon.
“You know that I’ve always been fiercely independent, and I will continue to be that for you for as long as I am here and beyond,” she said. “That’s especially important today as we face unprecedented pressures from all sides – political, financial, and also from the rising dangers in the field.”
In his own memo, CNN’s CEO, Mark Thompson, who announced earlier this month that he will be remaining with the merged company, thanked Amanpour “for 43 extraordinary years of remarkable journalism, loyalty and friendship”.
“Christiane has thought carefully about this decision, and she and I have been discussing it for some months,” Thompson wrote. “Like so many CNNers who will hear the news today, I’m very sorry to see her go, but I’ve come to accept that this is the right time for her, both personally and professionally.”
Amanpour said she will continue hosting her podcast, The Ex Files and that she “[looks] forward to interesting new projects down the line”.

articles.title: France hit by debt sell-off as violent protests unnerve investors
articles.summary: Difference between French and German borrowing costs widens after public buildings burned and shops lootedFrance has been hit by a fresh wave of selling in its bond and stock markets after violent protests over the weekend led to thousands of arrests and left public buildings burned and hundreds of shops looted across the country.The chaos has spooked investors as analysts worried that it would undermine Paris’s efforts to cut spending and reduce its debt. Continue reading...
articles.full_text:
France has been hit by a fresh wave of selling in its bond and stock markets after violent protests over the weekend led to thousands of arrests and left public buildings burned and hundreds of shops looted across the country.
The chaos has spooked investors as analysts worried that it would undermine Paris’s efforts to cut spending and reduce its debt.
The yield on the government’s 10-year bonds rose by as much as 16 basis points to 4.94% on Monday. Yields rise when prices fall, and the bond market sell-off pushed France’s borrowing costs close to a 24-year high.
This widened the difference between the French and German 10-year borrowing costs – which is a metric for the risk premium attached to French debt – towards its highest level in 14 years.
Analysts at Goldman Sachs said European sovereign risk was back in focus, with fiscal concerns about France raising the question of whether there could be a repeat of the eurozone debt crisis of 15 years ago.
“The risks of disorderly market escalation and real economy contagion look notably lower. But the fundamental fiscal challenges for some countries – especially in France – look harder now than in 2011-15,” the investment bank said.
“The issue of how to deal with fundamental sovereign risk remains unresolved in the euro area, requiring credible fiscal consolidation.”
The two-year French bond yield rose by nine basis points to 3.64%.
Concerns about France’s instability knocked the euro down to a 17-month low against the pound on Monday morning, when sterling rose to €1.188.
Violence erupted across France after weeks of relatively peaceful demonstrations over conditions in schools and the cost of living, prompting the French president, Emmanuel Macron, to condemn the “unbridled violence” in a televised address on Sunday night.
Tens of thousands of people have attended peaceful marches to demand more teachers and repairs to decrepit schools, but different groups have clashed with police in cities including Paris, Bordeaux, Nice and Marseille.
Jim Reid of Deutsche Bank said the protests “won’t make it easy for the international community to be totally comfortable buying OATs”, referring to French government bonds.
“With France already facing a difficult fiscal backdrop and the 2027 election approaching, the weekend adds another layer of political risk for markets,” he said.
The 30-year bond, which is a benchmark for the French government’s long-term cost of borrowing, rose by ten basis points to 5.46%.
The rises will put further strain on France’s public finances as the government tries to pass a budget for next year to rein in its deficit.
France’s debt-to-GDP stood at 115.6% in 2025, while its budget deficit was 5.1%, compared with 94.3% and 4.3% respectively for the UK.
The unrest adds to “concerns about the political and fiscal troubles in France”, said Neil Wilson, Saxo UK’s investor strategist.
“It underscores how hard it will be for a government to enact the kind of spending restraint required to get the deficit down.”
The French government is preparing a budget that would involve cutting pensions spending and funding for government departments, excluding defence. There are growing fears, however, that political pressure could derail the plans, which could push up borrowing further and add more to the country’s debt pile.
The euro also slipped against the US dollar, down by 0.4% at one stage on Monday to $1.1197.
France’s Cac 40 index, which tracks the biggest companies listed in Paris, fell by 1.4% , compared with a 1.1% drop on the pan-European Stoxx 600 index.
French bank stocks were among the fallers, with Société Générale and BNP Paribas down more than 3%.
Other European stock markets also weakened, with Italy’s FTSE Mib down 1.6% and Spain’s Ibex dropping by 1.9%.
Daniela Hathorn, a senior market analyst at Capital.com, said investors were concerned that higher borrowing costs would increase France’s debt-servicing expenses, reducing its fiscal flexibility at a time when growth is already subdued.
“But France is not alone,” he said. “Spain faces its own political constraints around budgets and fiscal reforms, although stronger economic growth provides some protection, while Italy’s substantial debt stock leaves it particularly sensitive to prolonged periods of elevated yields.”

articles.title: AI firm Anthropic to commit 5% of shares to fund for ‘public good’
articles.summary: The $48bn giveaway comes amid concerns about the tech and as the company prepares for a stock market listingAnthropic has said it will commit 5% of its shares to a fund for the “public good”, as the AI developer behind the Claude chatbot seeks to bolster its appeal before its stock market listing.The company announced it would commit the shares, worth around $48bn (£36bn) at its latest valuation in May, subject to shareholder approval. It will add a further 2% of its stock to the fund for every ...
articles.full_text:
Anthropic has said it will commit 5% of its shares to a fund for the “public good”, as the AI developer behind the Claude chatbot seeks to bolster its appeal before its stock market listing.
The company announced it would commit the shares, worth around $48bn (£36bn) at its latest valuation in May, subject to shareholder approval. It will add a further 2% of its stock to the fund for every 50% increase in its value above an undisclosed baseline.
The fund will allow Anthropic to “explore large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations”, the company said.
The move comes amid growing public nervousness about AI, from the threat to human labour to the impact on the environment and its influence on social behaviours.
“AI may generate enormous economic value, but it could also cause instability for many workers,” Anthropic wrote in a blogpost.
It said that while it had already committed $200m to addressing the issue, “given the pace of AI progress, bolder approaches may be needed. The fund will have the versatility to pursue them.”
The company, which is preparing to list on the stock market, has called for a slowdown in breakneck development of AI, a warning later echoed by rivals such as OpenAI.
Anthropic was valued at $965bn in May when it raised $65bn in a funding round. The company is reportedly considering a $1.5tn valuation when it floats on the stock market, with an IPO planned for November.
Last week, Anthropic said some of its AI models could soon become “self-replicating” and find ways to infiltrate internet-connected devices such as smart fridges and automatic vacuum cleaners.
It said that once this happens, the models would be able to power themselves without the need of datacentres.
Elon Musk, the chief executive of Tesla and founder of SpaceX, responded to Anthropic’s plans for a public benefit fund on social media by pledging to give some of his own shares away.
“I recommend giving the shares directly to the public,” he wrote. “This is what I will be doing.”
He later announced: “Next year, I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America. This will be the first of many.”
Shares in SpaceX, which is listed on the Nasdaq in the US, rose by 1% in pre-market trading on Monday. The company has lost about 9% of its value since it joined the stock market in June.
OpenAI, the developer behind ChatGPT, also reportedly engaged in early talks to give a 5% stake in its organisation to the US government.
Anthropic, which was founded in 2021 by seven former OpenAI employees, was established as a public benefit corporation. It means that all of the company’s directors must balance financial returns with its public interest mission.
